Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 34, verse 10–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We bestowed upon David grace from Us: "O mountains, echo [God's praises] with him"﴾. Its meaning: and We said, "O mountains, echo [God's praises] with him":

Glorify [God] with him when he glorifies. Abu Maysara said: it is in the language of Abyssinia (al-Habasha). Others said: it is the taf'il form from al-iyab (return), meaning: return with him in glorification. This is the meaning of the statement of Qatada and Abu 'Ubayd. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "Lament with him."

﴿And the birds﴾ [also, i.e., they should help you in that]. He said: When he called out in lamentation, the mountains responded to him with their echoes, and the birds gathered around him from above; so the echo of the mountains that people hear is from that day.

It is said: when David glorified God, the mountains would respond to him with glorification in the same manner as he glorified. Then one night he said to himself: "I will worship God, Exalted is He, with a worship no one has worshipped with its like." So he ascended the mountain. When it was the middle of the night and he was on the mountain, loneliness overcame him, so God, glorified is He, revealed to the mountains: "Give David company." He said: So the mountains shook with glorification and declaration of God's unity (tahlil). David said to himself: "How can my voice be heard amid these voices?" Then an angel descended to him and took hold of his arm until he brought him to the sea. He kicked it with his foot, and the sea parted for him. He brought him to the earth, and he kicked it with his foot, and the earth split open for him, until he brought him to the fish. He kicked it with his foot, and it moved aside from a rock; he kicked the rock with his foot, and it cracked, and from it emerged a worm that was stirring. The angel said to him: "Your Lord hears the stirring of this worm in this place."

Al-Qutabi said: its origin is from al-ta'wib in travel, which is to travel all day and stop at night.

Ibn Muqbil said:

"We reached a tribe who kept traveling on after the sun's rays had been pushed back, while the eye was drooping."

It is as if he meant: persist throughout the day in glorifying with him. It was also said: travel with him however he wills.

﴿And the birds﴾ is the reading of the majority with the accusative. It has two aspects: first, as a verb, its meaning being: "And We subjected the birds to him," like your saying: "I fed him food and water," meaning "and I gave him water to drink." The second aspect is the vocative, like your saying: "O 'Amr and al-Salt, come forward," where you put al-Salt in the accusative because he is called with the particle of address; when it is missing, he is as if turned away from his direction, so he is put in the accusative. It was also said: "together with the birds," so the birds are commanded to travel along with him.

It is transmitted from Ya'qub with the nominative, in response to "the mountains," meaning: "O mountains, echo with him, you and the birds," like the statement of the poet:

"Ala ya 'Amr wa al-Dahhak, sira, fa-qad jawaztuma khamr al-tariq."
(Oh 'Amr and al-Dahhak, go on, for you have passed the thick of the road.)

It is permissible to put al-Dahhak in the accusative or the nominative.

His saying: ﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾. He mentioned that the iron was in his hand like wet clay, dough, and wax; he shaped it with his hand as he willed, without fire or striking with iron. The cause of this, as related in the reports, was that when David (peace be upon him) became king over the Children of Israel, it was his custom to go out to the people in disguise. When he saw a man he did not recognize, he would approach him and ask him about David, saying: "What do you say about David, and about you, what sort of man is this?" They would praise him and say: "He is good among us."

While he was doing this one day, God sent an angel in the form of a human. When David saw him, he approached him as was his custom and asked him. The angel said to him: "He is an excellent man, were it not for one trait in him." David was disturbed by this and said: "What is it, servant of God?" He said: "He eats and feeds his dependents from the public treasury." He said: So David became alert to this, and asked God, Exalted is He, to provide him a means by which he might be independent of the public treasury, so that he could earn his living from it and feed his dependents. So God made iron soft for him, and it became in his hand like wax, and He taught him the craft of making coats of mail, and he would make coats of mail, and he was the first to make them.

It is said that he would sell each coat for four thousand, eating and feeding his dependents from it and giving charity from it to the poor and needy. It is also said: He made iron soft in his hand because of the strength that had been given to him.

﴿That make full coats of mail and measure well the links﴾, i.e., do not make the rivets too fine, lest they come loose, nor too thick, lest they break the rings. So he would do that. He was the first to make coats of mail; before that they were plates. Al-sard means the craft of making a coat of mail, and from it the craftsman is called sarrad and zarrad, and a coat of mail is called masrudah. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"And upon them two woven coats, which David or the craft of the ample coats of Tubba' completed."

Its origin is connection and arrangement, and from it the beads are called sard, and the awl is called misrad and sarrad. Al-Shammakh said:

"As the strands of the rein follow the wide-stitched ones..." and sard al-kalam (the arrangement of speech).

﴿And work righteousness﴾, meaning David and his family. ﴿Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 34, verse 12–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind" (al-rih). The common reading is with a fatha on the ḥā' (al-rīḥa), meaning: "And We subjected the wind to Sulayman." Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal related from ʿĀṣim a reading with a ḍammah (al-rīḥu), on the basis of the preposition of accompaniment being understood (the phrase being in the nominative, with the sense of "and for Sulayman was the wind").

"Its morning course is a month, and its evening course is a month": from midday until night is a month's journey. [Mā] [[An addition required by the context.]] So it carries him in a single day over the distance of two months' journey.

Wahb said: It was mentioned to me that on a dwelling in the region of the Tigris there was written an inscription [written] [[In the manuscript: kataba-hu.]] by one of the companions of Sulayman (peace be upon him), whether from among the jinn or from among mankind: "By a sea we descended, and we did not build it; built, we found it. We set out in the morning from Istakhr and we said, and we are returning from it, God willing, and will spend the night in Syria."

al-Hasan said: When the horses occupied Prophet Sulayman son of Dawud to the point that he missed the ʿAṣr prayer, he became angry for God's sake and slaughtered (ʿaqara) the horses. God the Exalted replaced them for him with something better and quicker: they run at his command however he wills, "its morning course is a month and its evening course is a month." He would set out from Iliya, take a midday rest at Istakhr, then depart from there and arrive in the evening at Kabul.

Ibn Zayd said: He (peace be upon him) had a vessel of wood, and in it were a thousand pillars, and at each pillar a thousand chambers; with him there rode in it men from the jinn and mankind, and beneath each pillar a thousand devils who lifted that vessel. When it rose, the gentle wind came and carried it along with them. He would take his midday rest among a people with a month's distance between him and them, and his evening rest among another people with a month's distance between him and them, so the people would not know until the armies had overshadowed them.

It is related that Sulayman (peace be upon him) journeyed from the land of Iraq in the morning and stopped at the city of Marw, and prayed ʿAṣr in the city of Balkh, carried by the wind with his soldiers, and the birds shading them. Then he travelled from the city of Balkh, passing through the lands of the Turks, then passed beyond them to the land of China, going out in the morning a month's distance and returning in the evening a similar distance. Then he turned to the right from the rising of the sun along the seashore until he reached the land of Qandahar, and went out from it to Makran and Kirman, then passed beyond them until he reached the land of Persia and stayed there some days, and set out in the morning and stopped at Kaskar, then returned to Syria, and his residence was in the city of Tadmur. The devils had, before his departure from Syria to Iraq, been ordered by him to build it, so they built it for him with slabs of stone, columns, and white and yellow marble. Concerning that, al-Nabigha says:

"Behold Sulayman, when the God said to him: 'Rise up in the wilderness and clear it of the ...'
And subdue the jinn, for I have permitted them: they build Tadmur with slabs and columns."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 13/121 and Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 14/269.]]

I found these verses carved on a rock in the land of Kaskar, composed by one of the companions of Sulayman son of Dawud (peace be upon them both):

"We, and there is no might save the might of our Lord, return to our homelands from the land of Tadmur.
When we return, the time of our rest is a month's journey, and the morning of the next [is a month's journey].
People who sold their souls to God willingly, for the victory of the son of Dawud, the purified Prophet.
For them is virtue and elevation in the lofty matters of religion, and if they are ever traced, they are of the best of tribes.
Whenever they mount the obedient wind, it hastens, swift, not falling short of its month.
Birds in ranks shade them; whenever they flutter above them, they do not startle."

His saying: "And We caused the spring of copper to flow for him" (ʿayn al-qiṭr): We melted for him the copper ore, which flowed for him for three days as water flows. It was in the land of Yemen, and people benefit today from what God brought forth for Sulayman.

"And whoever deviates" (yazigh): turns away and swerves "from Our command" which We commanded him, of obedience to Sulayman, "We shall make him taste the punishment of the blaze" (al-saʿir) in the Hereafter. This is the view of most exegetes, while some said it is in this world: God the Exalted had appointed over them an angel holding a whip of fire, so whoever deviated from the command of Sulayman, he struck with a blow that burned him.

"They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries" (maḥārīb): places of worship, dwellings, and palaces. The maḥrāb is the front of every masjid, and a majlis (assembly) and a house. ʿAdi said:

"Like dolls of ivory in the sanctuaries, or like eggs in the meadow, its flower [shining] [[So in the sources of the tafsir, see Tafsir al-Tabari; it is the correct metre; in the manuscript: mustakbir.]]"

Among what they made for him of that was the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Its story and description, as mentioned by the people of expertise in histories, is that God the Exalted blessed the progeny of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) until He made them numerous beyond counting. When the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) came, he remained among them thirty years in the land of Palestine, and they increased in number every day, so Dawud was pleased by their multitude and ordered them counted. They kept counting for a period of time until they despaired and were unable to encompass the number of the Children of Israel. God revealed to Dawud: "I had promised your father Ibrahim on the day I commanded him to slaughter his son that he would be truthful to Me and carry out My command, and that I would bless his offspring until they become more than the number of the stars of the heaven and until those who count cannot enumerate them. I have sworn to test them with a calamity by which their number will diminish and your pride in their multitude will depart from you." He gave him the choice between punishing them with hunger and famine for three years, or letting their enemy overpower them for three months, or sending the plague upon them for three days.

Dawud gathered the Children of Israel and informed them of what God had revealed to him and of the choice given to him in it. They said: "You know best what is easier for us, and you are our prophet, so decide for us. Only, we have no patience with hunger, and the enemy's domination is a disgraceful matter; if it must be, then death." So Dawud (peace be upon him) commanded them to prepare themselves for death, so they washed, perfumed themselves, put on shrouds, and went out to the open ground with their children and families, and he ordered them to cry out to God and beseech Him, perhaps [[In the manuscript there is an addition: "that"]] He would have mercy on them. That was in the open ground of Bayt al-Maqdis before the building of the mosque.

He said: Dawud (peace be upon him) ascended above the rock, then fell down prostrating, supplicating to God the Exalted, and God sent the plague upon them. In one day and night it destroyed of them such a number that they were not free from burying them until after a period of two months. When they awoke on the second day, Dawud prostrated and they prostrated with him until the sun rose, and they did not lift their heads until God lifted the plague from them.

They said: When God the Exalted interceded for the Children of Israel through Dawud at that place, Dawud gathered the Children of Israel after three days and said to them: "God the Holy has bestowed grace upon you and shown you mercy, so renew your thanks to Him." They said: "How do you command us?" He said: "I command you to take from this open ground, upon which He has shown you mercy, a mosque in which there will always remain from you and from those after you one who remembers."

When they intended to build, a righteous poor man came to test them, to know how sincere they were in their steadfastness. He said to the Children of Israel: "I have a place in it that I need, and it is not lawful for you to keep me from it." They said to him: "O man, there is no one among the Children of Israel who does not have in this open ground a right like your right, so do not be the most miserly of people nor constrict us in it." He said: "I do not know my right, and you do not know it." They said to him: "Either you be content and be at ease in soul, or we will take it from you by force." He said to them: "Or do you find that in the judgment of God and in the judgment of Dawud?"

He said: They raised his report to Dawud, and he said: "Satisfy him." They said: "For how much shall we take it, O Prophet of God?" He said: "Take it for a hundred sheep." The man said: "Add." Dawud said: "For a hundred cows." He said: "Add." He said: "A hundred camels." He said: "Add to me, for what you are buying is for God the Exalted." Dawud said: "As for when you say this, then name your price and I will give it to you." He said: "Buy from me an orchard like it, of olives, date palms and grapes." He said: "Yes." He said: "Buy it for God, and do not be stingy." He said: "Ask what you will and I will give it to you, or if you wish I will hire myself out to you." He said: "And would you do that, O Prophet of God?" He said: "Yes, if you wish." He said:

"You are more honoured before God than that. Rather, build around it a high wall and fill it with gold, or silver if you wish."

Dawud said: "It is easy."

Then the man turned to the Children of Israel and said: "This is the sincere repentant." Then he said to Dawud: "O Prophet of God, that God should forgive me one sin is dearer to me than everything He has given me, but I was testing you."

So they set about building Bayt al-Maqdis, and Dawud (peace be upon him) would carry the stones for them upon his shoulder, as did the best of the Children of Israel, until they raised it to the height of a man. Then God the Exalted revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him): "This is a holy house, and you are a man who sheds blood a great deal, so you shall not build it unless I decree that by your hand. But a son of yours who will reign after you, named Sulayman, I will make him free of shedding blood, and I will decree its completion by his hand; and that will be his fame and his remembrance for you, lasting."

They prayed in it for a time, and Dawud was then a son of one hundred and twenty-seven years. When he reached the age of one hundred and forty years, God took him, and Sulayman succeeded him. He loved building Bayt al-Maqdis, so he gathered the jinn and the devils and divided the labours among them, assigning each group to a task suited to it. He sent the jinn and the devils to obtain marble and pure white al-mahā from their mines, and commanded that the city be built with marble and slabs. He made it twelve quarters (arbād), and settled in each quarter one of the tribes, and they were twelve tribes.

When he finished building the city, he began building the mosque. He directed the devils in groups: some extracting gold, silver and rubies from their mines and pure pearls from the sea; some tearing out jewels and stones from their places; and some bringing musk and ambergris. Of that there came a quantity that none can count but God the Exalted. Then he summoned the craftsmen and ordered them to cut those raised stones and shape them into slabs, and to prepare those jewels and drill the rubies and pearls. They were working on them, and they made a loud sound because of their hardness, and Sulayman disliked those sounds. He called the jinn and said to them: "Do you have a device for cutting these jewels without noise?"

They said: "O Messenger of God, there is none among the jinn with more experience nor more knowledge than Sakhr al-ʿIfrit. Send for him and he will bring it to you." So Sulayman sealed his ring with a seal (he used to seal the devils with copper and the rest of the jinn with iron), and whenever he sealed one of them with his ring, it shone like a flashing lightning, so no one saw it:

"No jinn nor devil but yielded to him, by the permission of God, mighty is His power."

He sent the seal with ten of the jinn, and they came to him while he was on some island in the seas. They showed him the seal, and when he looked at it he nearly fainted from fear; so he came hastening with the messengers until he entered upon Sulayman (peace be upon him). Sulayman asked his messengers what the ifrit had done on his way. They said: "O Messenger of God, he used to laugh at some of the people at times." Sulayman (peace be upon him) said to him: "Were you not content with your rebellion against me, in not coming to me in obedience, until you began to mock people?"

He said: "O Prophet of God, I did not mock them, except that my laughter was out of wonder at what I heard and saw on my way." Sulayman said: "And what was that?"

He said: "Know that I passed by a man on the bank of a river, with a mule that he wished to water, and with him a jug with which he wished to draw water. He watered the mule and filled the jug, then he wanted to relieve himself, so he tied the mule by the handle of the jug; the mule bolted and dragged the jug and broke it. I laughed at the folly of the man, for he imagined that the jug would hold back the mule.

"And I passed by a man sitting beside a cobbler whom he hired to repair a shoe of his; I heard him stipulate with him that he repair it so that it would last four years, and he forgot that death might come upon him before that. I laughed at his heedlessness and ignorance.

"And I passed by an old woman who was soothsaying and telling people what they did not know of the affairs of the heavens, and I had known that a man had buried a great deal of gold in the place of her bed in past ages. I saw her dying of hunger while under her bed was much gold, of whose place she did not know; then she tells people about the affairs of the heavens, so I laughed at her.

"And I passed by a man in some town, who had an illness, it is said, and he ate onions and was cured of his illness, and he began to practise medicine for people; whoever came to him asking about an ailment, he commanded him to eat onions, and they are the most harmful of things, to the point that their harm reaches the brain. So I laughed at him.

"And I passed by some markets, and I saw garlic, which is the best of all remedies, being sold by measure, and I saw pepper, which is one of the deadly poisons, being sold by weight; so I laughed at that.

"And I passed by people who had sat supplicating God the Exalted and asking Him for forgiveness and mercy; some of them grew weary and got up, and others came and sat, and I saw mercy descend upon them. The mercy missed those who were of the original assembly and overtook those who came and sat; so I laughed in wonder at the decree and the destiny."

They said: Sulayman said to him: "Have you, in your great experience and your wanderings on land and sea, known of anything with which these jewels can be cut, so that it softens and their cutting and drilling become easy without noise?" He said: "Yes, O Prophet of God, I know a white stone like milk called al-samur, but I do not know the mine in which it is found; and among birds there is nothing more clever nor more guided than the eagle. Order an eagle to have its chicks placed in a box of stone with it for a night; then release that eagle and leave its chicks in the box, and it will certainly bring that stone and strike with it the back of the box until it breaks through, so as to reach its chicks."

He said: Sulayman commanded an eagle with its chicks; he placed it in a box of stone for a day and a night, then released the eagle without the chicks. The eagle went off and came back with that stone after a day and a night, and broke the box with it until it reached its chicks. Sulayman sent with the eagle a band of the jinn until they brought him from it an amount that he knew was sufficient, and he used that for the craftsmen's tools, so that cutting became easy for them without noise. It is the stone used to engrave rings and drill jewels to this day, and it is a rare and precious stone.

He said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) built the mosque with white, yellow and green marble, and supported it with columns of pure al-mahā, and roofed it with slabs of precious jewels, and inlaid its ceilings and walls with pearls, rubies and all kinds of jewels, and paved its floor with slabs of turquoise. There was not on earth at that time a house more splendid or brighter than that mosque; it shone in the darkness like the moon on the night of the full moon.

When he finished it, he gathered to him the best of the Children of Israel and informed them that he had built it for God, and that everything in it was purely for God; and he made the day on which he finished it a festival.

They also said: Among the wonders that Sulayman (peace be upon him) made in Bayt al-Maqdis is that he built a house and plastered its wall with green clay and polished it; whenever a pious, righteous person entered it, his image appeared white on that wall, and whenever a wicked, dissolute person entered, his image appeared black on it. Many people then refrained from immorality and treachery.

In one corner of the mosque he set up a staff of ebony; whoever touched it of the sons of the prophets, its touch did not harm him, and whoever touched it of others, his hand burned.

Al-Awza'i related from Rabi'ah ibn Yazid from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Daylami from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When Sulayman finished building Bayt al-Maqdis, he asked his Lord for three things, and He gave him two, and I hope that God has given him the third: he asked for a judgment that would coincide with His judgment, and He gave it to him; he asked for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, and He gave it to him; and he asked that no one who comes to this house and prays two rak'ahs in it would leave his sins behind, like the day his mother bore him, and I hope that He has given him that." [31] [[Al-Mustadrak: 2/434, with slight variation.]]

They said: Bayt al-Maqdis remained as Sulayman (peace be upon him) built it, until Nebuchadnezzar invaded, destroyed the city and demolished it, dismantled the mosque, and took what was in its ceilings and walls of gold, silver, pearls, rubies and all kinds of jewels, and carried it with him to the seat of his kingdom in the land of Iraq.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: When Sulayman finished building Bayt al-Maqdis, its doors were locked; Sulayman tried them but they would not open, until in his supplication he said: "By the prayers of Abu Dawud, open the doors!" So they opened. Sulayman appointed for it ten thousand of the Qur'an-reciters of the Children of Israel: five thousand by night and five thousand by day, so that no hour of night or day passed without God being worshipped in it.

Tamathil (images) means pictures; they made images in the mosques of copper, brass, tin, glass and marble, images of angels and righteous prophets, so that when people saw them depicted they would worship as they worshipped.

Jifan (basins) means bowls, their singular being jafnah. Kal-jawab (like cisterns) means like the reservoirs into which water is gathered, that is, collected; its singular is jabiyah.

al-Acsha Maymun ibn Qays said:

"He goes forth over the family of Mikhlaq with a bowl, like the cistern of the Iraqi elder, overflowing."

Ibn Hamid? No—here is the translation.

Abu Bakr al-Hamshawi informed us, saying: Abu Bakr al-Qati'i Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah ibn Muslim informed me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Sahl al-Sarraj narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Hasan say: (wa-jifanin ka-l-jawab) "like the watering troughs of camels." It is said that a thousand men would gather around one single bowl, eating before him.

Wa-qudurin rasiyat: fixed in place, not moved or shifted from their positions because of their enormity, and not taken down or left unused. They were in Yemen, and from the same root comes the term for mountains, rawasi (firmly fixed ones).

I'malu aal Dawud shukran: that is, "We said: Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude," meaning: work in obedience to God, O family of Dawud, in thanks for His blessings. Shukran is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar).

Wa-qalilun min ibadiya al-shakur: Hamzah read it with a sukun on the ya' (yā’), and the rest read it with a fatha. Al-Qurazi said: gratitude (shukr) is fear of God and acting in obedience to Him.

They also narrated to us on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, saying: al-Hasr ibn Aban narrated to us, saying: Sayyar narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Thabit say: Dawud, the Prophet of God (peace be upon him), had divided the hours of the night and day among his family, so that at no hour of the night or day was there not someone from the family of Dawud standing in prayer. Thus God included them all in this verse: I'malu aal Dawud shukran.

Fa-lamma qadayna alayhi al-mawt: The exegetes said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) would seclude himself in Bayt al-Maqdis for a year, two years, a month, two months, or less or more, and his food and drink would be brought in to him. He entered it on the occasion in which he died. The sign of this was that every morning a tree would sprout in Bayt al-Maqdis, and he would ask it: "What is your name?" The tree would say: "My name is such-and-such." He would say: "For what purpose are you?" It would say: "For such-and-such." Then he would order it cut down. If it had sprouted for planting, he would plant it; if it was for medicine, it would be recorded.

Then one day, while he was praying, he saw a tree before him, and he said to it: "What is your name?" It said: "Al-Kharrubah (the carob)." He said: "For what purpose did you sprout?" It said: "For the ruin of this mosque." Sulayman said: "God would not ruin it while I am alive. You are the one on whose account my death and the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis will come." He uprooted it, planted it in a courtyard of his, then said: "O God, conceal my death from the jinn, so that mankind will know that the jinn do not know the unseen," for the jinn used to tell mankind that they knew some of the unseen and what would happen tomorrow. Then he entered the prayer niche (mihrab) and stood praying, leaning on his staff, and he died.

Ibn Zayd said: Sulayman said to the Angel of Death: "When you are commanded concerning me, inform me." So he came to him and said: "O Sulayman, I have been commanded concerning you, and only a short while remains for you."

He summoned the devils, and they built around him a palace of glass with no door. He stood praying, leaning on his staff, and the Angel of Death entered upon him and seized his soul while he was leaning on his staff.

In another narration: Sulayman (peace be upon him) said one day to his companions: "God has given me the kingdom that you see, and no day has passed over me in my rule in which it was clear of turbidity. I have wished that I might have one day that is clear for me until night, in which I am not grieved; but that day is tomorrow."

When the next day came, he entered one of his palaces and ordered its doors to be closed, and prevented people from entering upon him, and kept news from reaching him, lest he hear anything on that day that would distress him. Then he took his staff in hand, climbed to the top of his palace, and leaned on his staff, looking over his kingdoms. Suddenly he saw a young man of handsome face, wearing white garments, who had come upon him from one side of his palace. He said: "Peace be upon you, O Sulayman." He said: "And upon you peace. How did you enter this palace, when you were forbidden to enter it? Did the gatekeeper and the chamberlains not prevent you? Did you not stand in awe of me when you entered my palace without my permission?" He said: "I am one whom no chamberlain can hold back, and no doorkeeper can repel, and I do not fear kings, nor do I accept bribes, and I would not have entered this palace without permission." Sulayman said: "Who gave you permission to enter it?" He said: "Its Lord."

Sulayman trembled and knew that he was the Angel of Death. He said to him: "Are you the Angel of Death?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then for what have you come?" He said: "I have come to seize your soul." He said: "O Angel of Death, this is a day I wished would be clear for me, and that I would not hear in it anything that grieves me." He said: "O Sulayman, you wished for a day in which your life would be clear and in which you would not be grieved. That day has not been created among the days of this world. So be content with the decree of your Lord, for it has no reversal."

He said: "Then carry out what you were commanded."

The Angel of Death seized his soul while he was leaning on his staff. They said: the devils used to gather around his prayer niche and place of prayer wherever he was. The prayer niche had openings (kuwwa) before him and behind him, and a devil who wanted to leave would say: "Am I not bold enough? If I enter and exit from that side..." and he would enter and exit from the other side. One of those devils entered, passed through, and did not hear Sulayman's voice; then he returned and did not hear it; then he returned and fell into the room, but was not burned. He looked at Sulayman, who had fallen dead. So he went out and informed the people that Sulayman had died. They opened the place for him and brought him out, and they found his staff, which in the Abyssinian tongue is "minsa'ah," eaten by termites. They did not know how long he had been dead, so they placed termites on the staff, and it was eaten by them for a day and a night. Then they calculated accordingly and found that he had been dead for a year. The jinn had been working before him, looking at him and thinking he was alive, and they did not notice his absence from going out to the people because of his long prayer before that. [Tafsir al-Tabari 22/92; Tarikh al-Tabari 1/356.]

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "They continued toiling for him a full year after his death." The people then realized that the jinn had been lying to them, and that if they had known the unseen they would have known of Sulayman's death and would not have remained in humiliating torment, working for him for a year. Then the devils said to the termite: "If you ate food, we would bring you the finest food, and if you drank drink, we would give you the finest drink, but we will transport mud and water to you." So they carried these to it wherever it was. He said: Have you not seen the mud that is on wood? It is from what the devils bring to it, out of gratitude to it. This is the meaning of God's words: Fa-lamma qadayna alayhi al-mawt ma dallahum ala mawtihi illa dabbat al-ard, which is the termite. It is also called al-qadih, and it is a small creature that eats wood.

Ta'kulu minsa'atahu: that is, his staff. Its root is from "nasa'a al-ghanam," when one drives and herds the sheep. Tarafah said:

"Strong, like boards of Aran wood, I drove her on a road like the back of a striped cloak."

That is, I drove her. Most readers pronounce the hamza, while Abu Amr and the people of Medina leave it unpronounced, and both are dialects. A poet who used the hamza said:

"We struck with a staff his face, so he became humiliated and abased thereby."

Others, who left out the hamza, said:

"If you walk upon the staff in old age, then idle talk and dalliance have departed far from you."

His words: Fa-lamma kharra tabayyanat al-jinnu an law kanu ya'lamuna al-ghayba ma labithu fi al-adhab al-muhin. The "an" is in the nominative position, because the meaning is: when he fell, it became clear and was revealed that, had the jinn... i.e., their situation became manifest. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "an law kana al-jinnu yalamuna al-ghayba ma labithu fi al-adhab al-muhin." It is also said that "an" is in the accusative position, meaning: the jinn knew and were certain that, had they known the unseen...

The historians said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) lived fifty-three years, and his reign lasted forty years. He became king at the age of thirteen, and he began building Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 34, verse 12–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind" (al-rih). The common reading is with a fatha on the ḥā' (al-rīḥa), meaning: "And We subjected the wind to Sulayman." Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal related from ʿĀṣim a reading with a ḍammah (al-rīḥu), on the basis of the preposition of accompaniment being understood (the phrase being in the nominative, with the sense of "and for Sulayman was the wind").

"Its morning course is a month, and its evening course is a month": from midday until night is a month's journey. [Mā] [[An addition required by the context.]] So it carries him in a single day over the distance of two months' journey.

Wahb said: It was mentioned to me that on a dwelling in the region of the Tigris there was written an inscription [written] [[In the manuscript: kataba-hu.]] by one of the companions of Sulayman (peace be upon him), whether from among the jinn or from among mankind: "By a sea we descended, and we did not build it; built, we found it. We set out in the morning from Istakhr and we said, and we are returning from it, God willing, and will spend the night in Syria."

al-Hasan said: When the horses occupied Prophet Sulayman son of Dawud to the point that he missed the ʿAṣr prayer, he became angry for God's sake and slaughtered (ʿaqara) the horses. God the Exalted replaced them for him with something better and quicker: they run at his command however he wills, "its morning course is a month and its evening course is a month." He would set out from Iliya, take a midday rest at Istakhr, then depart from there and arrive in the evening at Kabul.

Ibn Zayd said: He (peace be upon him) had a vessel of wood, and in it were a thousand pillars, and at each pillar a thousand chambers; with him there rode in it men from the jinn and mankind, and beneath each pillar a thousand devils who lifted that vessel. When it rose, the gentle wind came and carried it along with them. He would take his midday rest among a people with a month's distance between him and them, and his evening rest among another people with a month's distance between him and them, so the people would not know until the armies had overshadowed them.

It is related that Sulayman (peace be upon him) journeyed from the land of Iraq in the morning and stopped at the city of Marw, and prayed ʿAṣr in the city of Balkh, carried by the wind with his soldiers, and the birds shading them. Then he travelled from the city of Balkh, passing through the lands of the Turks, then passed beyond them to the land of China, going out in the morning a month's distance and returning in the evening a similar distance. Then he turned to the right from the rising of the sun along the seashore until he reached the land of Qandahar, and went out from it to Makran and Kirman, then passed beyond them until he reached the land of Persia and stayed there some days, and set out in the morning and stopped at Kaskar, then returned to Syria, and his residence was in the city of Tadmur. The devils had, before his departure from Syria to Iraq, been ordered by him to build it, so they built it for him with slabs of stone, columns, and white and yellow marble. Concerning that, al-Nabigha says:

"Behold Sulayman, when the God said to him: 'Rise up in the wilderness and clear it of the ...'
And subdue the jinn, for I have permitted them: they build Tadmur with slabs and columns."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 13/121 and Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 14/269.]]

I found these verses carved on a rock in the land of Kaskar, composed by one of the companions of Sulayman son of Dawud (peace be upon them both):

"We, and there is no might save the might of our Lord, return to our homelands from the land of Tadmur.
When we return, the time of our rest is a month's journey, and the morning of the next [is a month's journey].
People who sold their souls to God willingly, for the victory of the son of Dawud, the purified Prophet.
For them is virtue and elevation in the lofty matters of religion, and if they are ever traced, they are of the best of tribes.
Whenever they mount the obedient wind, it hastens, swift, not falling short of its month.
Birds in ranks shade them; whenever they flutter above them, they do not startle."

His saying: "And We caused the spring of copper to flow for him" (ʿayn al-qiṭr): We melted for him the copper ore, which flowed for him for three days as water flows. It was in the land of Yemen, and people benefit today from what God brought forth for Sulayman.

"And whoever deviates" (yazigh): turns away and swerves "from Our command" which We commanded him, of obedience to Sulayman, "We shall make him taste the punishment of the blaze" (al-saʿir) in the Hereafter. This is the view of most exegetes, while some said it is in this world: God the Exalted had appointed over them an angel holding a whip of fire, so whoever deviated from the command of Sulayman, he struck with a blow that burned him.

"They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries" (maḥārīb): places of worship, dwellings, and palaces. The maḥrāb is the front of every masjid, and a majlis (assembly) and a house. ʿAdi said:

"Like dolls of ivory in the sanctuaries, or like eggs in the meadow, its flower [shining] [[So in the sources of the tafsir, see Tafsir al-Tabari; it is the correct metre; in the manuscript: mustakbir.]]"

Among what they made for him of that was the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Its story and description, as mentioned by the people of expertise in histories, is that God the Exalted blessed the progeny of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) until He made them numerous beyond counting. When the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) came, he remained among them thirty years in the land of Palestine, and they increased in number every day, so Dawud was pleased by their multitude and ordered them counted. They kept counting for a period of time until they despaired and were unable to encompass the number of the Children of Israel. God revealed to Dawud: "I had promised your father Ibrahim on the day I commanded him to slaughter his son that he would be truthful to Me and carry out My command, and that I would bless his offspring until they become more than the number of the stars of the heaven and until those who count cannot enumerate them. I have sworn to test them with a calamity by which their number will diminish and your pride in their multitude will depart from you." He gave him the choice between punishing them with hunger and famine for three years, or letting their enemy overpower them for three months, or sending the plague upon them for three days.

Dawud gathered the Children of Israel and informed them of what God had revealed to him and of the choice given to him in it. They said: "You know best what is easier for us, and you are our prophet, so decide for us. Only, we have no patience with hunger, and the enemy's domination is a disgraceful matter; if it must be, then death." So Dawud (peace be upon him) commanded them to prepare themselves for death, so they washed, perfumed themselves, put on shrouds, and went out to the open ground with their children and families, and he ordered them to cry out to God and beseech Him, perhaps [[In the manuscript there is an addition: "that"]] He would have mercy on them. That was in the open ground of Bayt al-Maqdis before the building of the mosque.

He said: Dawud (peace be upon him) ascended above the rock, then fell down prostrating, supplicating to God the Exalted, and God sent the plague upon them. In one day and night it destroyed of them such a number that they were not free from burying them until after a period of two months. When they awoke on the second day, Dawud prostrated and they prostrated with him until the sun rose, and they did not lift their heads until God lifted the plague from them.

They said: When God the Exalted interceded for the Children of Israel through Dawud at that place, Dawud gathered the Children of Israel after three days and said to them: "God the Holy has bestowed grace upon you and shown you mercy, so renew your thanks to Him." They said: "How do you command us?" He said: "I command you to take from this open ground, upon which He has shown you mercy, a mosque in which there will always remain from you and from those after you one who remembers."

When they intended to build, a righteous poor man came to test them, to know how sincere they were in their steadfastness. He said to the Children of Israel: "I have a place in it that I need, and it is not lawful for you to keep me from it." They said to him: "O man, there is no one among the Children of Israel who does not have in this open ground a right like your right, so do not be the most miserly of people nor constrict us in it." He said: "I do not know my right, and you do not know it." They said to him: "Either you be content and be at ease in soul, or we will take it from you by force." He said to them: "Or do you find that in the judgment of God and in the judgment of Dawud?"

He said: They raised his report to Dawud, and he said: "Satisfy him." They said: "For how much shall we take it, O Prophet of God?" He said: "Take it for a hundred sheep." The man said: "Add." Dawud said: "For a hundred cows." He said: "Add." He said: "A hundred camels." He said: "Add to me, for what you are buying is for God the Exalted." Dawud said: "As for when you say this, then name your price and I will give it to you." He said: "Buy from me an orchard like it, of olives, date palms and grapes." He said: "Yes." He said: "Buy it for God, and do not be stingy." He said: "Ask what you will and I will give it to you, or if you wish I will hire myself out to you." He said: "And would you do that, O Prophet of God?" He said: "Yes, if you wish." He said:

"You are more honoured before God than that. Rather, build around it a high wall and fill it with gold, or silver if you wish."

Dawud said: "It is easy."

Then the man turned to the Children of Israel and said: "This is the sincere repentant." Then he said to Dawud: "O Prophet of God, that God should forgive me one sin is dearer to me than everything He has given me, but I was testing you."

So they set about building Bayt al-Maqdis, and Dawud (peace be upon him) would carry the stones for them upon his shoulder, as did the best of the Children of Israel, until they raised it to the height of a man. Then God the Exalted revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him): "This is a holy house, and you are a man who sheds blood a great deal, so you shall not build it unless I decree that by your hand. But a son of yours who will reign after you, named Sulayman, I will make him free of shedding blood, and I will decree its completion by his hand; and that will be his fame and his remembrance for you, lasting."

They prayed in it for a time, and Dawud was then a son of one hundred and twenty-seven years. When he reached the age of one hundred and forty years, God took him, and Sulayman succeeded him. He loved building Bayt al-Maqdis, so he gathered the jinn and the devils and divided the labours among them, assigning each group to a task suited to it. He sent the jinn and the devils to obtain marble and pure white al-mahā from their mines, and commanded that the city be built with marble and slabs. He made it twelve quarters (arbād), and settled in each quarter one of the tribes, and they were twelve tribes.

When he finished building the city, he began building the mosque. He directed the devils in groups: some extracting gold, silver and rubies from their mines and pure pearls from the sea; some tearing out jewels and stones from their places; and some bringing musk and ambergris. Of that there came a quantity that none can count but God the Exalted. Then he summoned the craftsmen and ordered them to cut those raised stones and shape them into slabs, and to prepare those jewels and drill the rubies and pearls. They were working on them, and they made a loud sound because of their hardness, and Sulayman disliked those sounds. He called the jinn and said to them: "Do you have a device for cutting these jewels without noise?"

They said: "O Messenger of God, there is none among the jinn with more experience nor more knowledge than Sakhr al-ʿIfrit. Send for him and he will bring it to you." So Sulayman sealed his ring with a seal (he used to seal the devils with copper and the rest of the jinn with iron), and whenever he sealed one of them with his ring, it shone like a flashing lightning, so no one saw it:

"No jinn nor devil but yielded to him, by the permission of God, mighty is His power."

He sent the seal with ten of the jinn, and they came to him while he was on some island in the seas. They showed him the seal, and when he looked at it he nearly fainted from fear; so he came hastening with the messengers until he entered upon Sulayman (peace be upon him). Sulayman asked his messengers what the ifrit had done on his way. They said: "O Messenger of God, he used to laugh at some of the people at times." Sulayman (peace be upon him) said to him: "Were you not content with your rebellion against me, in not coming to me in obedience, until you began to mock people?"

He said: "O Prophet of God, I did not mock them, except that my laughter was out of wonder at what I heard and saw on my way." Sulayman said: "And what was that?"

He said: "Know that I passed by a man on the bank of a river, with a mule that he wished to water, and with him a jug with which he wished to draw water. He watered the mule and filled the jug, then he wanted to relieve himself, so he tied the mule by the handle of the jug; the mule bolted and dragged the jug and broke it. I laughed at the folly of the man, for he imagined that the jug would hold back the mule.

"And I passed by a man sitting beside a cobbler whom he hired to repair a shoe of his; I heard him stipulate with him that he repair it so that it would last four years, and he forgot that death might come upon him before that. I laughed at his heedlessness and ignorance.

"And I passed by an old woman who was soothsaying and telling people what they did not know of the affairs of the heavens, and I had known that a man had buried a great deal of gold in the place of her bed in past ages. I saw her dying of hunger while under her bed was much gold, of whose place she did not know; then she tells people about the affairs of the heavens, so I laughed at her.

"And I passed by a man in some town, who had an illness, it is said, and he ate onions and was cured of his illness, and he began to practise medicine for people; whoever came to him asking about an ailment, he commanded him to eat onions, and they are the most harmful of things, to the point that their harm reaches the brain. So I laughed at him.

"And I passed by some markets, and I saw garlic, which is the best of all remedies, being sold by measure, and I saw pepper, which is one of the deadly poisons, being sold by weight; so I laughed at that.

"And I passed by people who had sat supplicating God the Exalted and asking Him for forgiveness and mercy; some of them grew weary and got up, and others came and sat, and I saw mercy descend upon them. The mercy missed those who were of the original assembly and overtook those who came and sat; so I laughed in wonder at the decree and the destiny."

They said: Sulayman said to him: "Have you, in your great experience and your wanderings on land and sea, known of anything with which these jewels can be cut, so that it softens and their cutting and drilling become easy without noise?" He said: "Yes, O Prophet of God, I know a white stone like milk called al-samur, but I do not know the mine in which it is found; and among birds there is nothing more clever nor more guided than the eagle. Order an eagle to have its chicks placed in a box of stone with it for a night; then release that eagle and leave its chicks in the box, and it will certainly bring that stone and strike with it the back of the box until it breaks through, so as to reach its chicks."

He said: Sulayman commanded an eagle with its chicks; he placed it in a box of stone for a day and a night, then released the eagle without the chicks. The eagle went off and came back with that stone after a day and a night, and broke the box with it until it reached its chicks. Sulayman sent with the eagle a band of the jinn until they brought him from it an amount that he knew was sufficient, and he used that for the craftsmen's tools, so that cutting became easy for them without noise. It is the stone used to engrave rings and drill jewels to this day, and it is a rare and precious stone.

He said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) built the mosque with white, yellow and green marble, and supported it with columns of pure al-mahā, and roofed it with slabs of precious jewels, and inlaid its ceilings and walls with pearls, rubies and all kinds of jewels, and paved its floor with slabs of turquoise. There was not on earth at that time a house more splendid or brighter than that mosque; it shone in the darkness like the moon on the night of the full moon.

When he finished it, he gathered to him the best of the Children of Israel and informed them that he had built it for God, and that everything in it was purely for God; and he made the day on which he finished it a festival.

They also said: Among the wonders that Sulayman (peace be upon him) made in Bayt al-Maqdis is that he built a house and plastered its wall with green clay and polished it; whenever a pious, righteous person entered it, his image appeared white on that wall, and whenever a wicked, dissolute person entered, his image appeared black on it. Many people then refrained from immorality and treachery.

In one corner of the mosque he set up a staff of ebony; whoever touched it of the sons of the prophets, its touch did not harm him, and whoever touched it of others, his hand burned.

Al-Awza'i related from Rabi'ah ibn Yazid from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Daylami from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When Sulayman finished building Bayt al-Maqdis, he asked his Lord for three things, and He gave him two, and I hope that God has given him the third: he asked for a judgment that would coincide with His judgment, and He gave it to him; he asked for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, and He gave it to him; and he asked that no one who comes to this house and prays two rak'ahs in it would leave his sins behind, like the day his mother bore him, and I hope that He has given him that." [31] [[Al-Mustadrak: 2/434, with slight variation.]]

They said: Bayt al-Maqdis remained as Sulayman (peace be upon him) built it, until Nebuchadnezzar invaded, destroyed the city and demolished it, dismantled the mosque, and took what was in its ceilings and walls of gold, silver, pearls, rubies and all kinds of jewels, and carried it with him to the seat of his kingdom in the land of Iraq.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: When Sulayman finished building Bayt al-Maqdis, its doors were locked; Sulayman tried them but they would not open, until in his supplication he said: "By the prayers of Abu Dawud, open the doors!" So they opened. Sulayman appointed for it ten thousand of the Qur'an-reciters of the Children of Israel: five thousand by night and five thousand by day, so that no hour of night or day passed without God being worshipped in it.

Tamathil (images) means pictures; they made images in the mosques of copper, brass, tin, glass and marble, images of angels and righteous prophets, so that when people saw them depicted they would worship as they worshipped.

Jifan (basins) means bowls, their singular being jafnah. Kal-jawab (like cisterns) means like the reservoirs into which water is gathered, that is, collected; its singular is jabiyah.

al-Acsha Maymun ibn Qays said:

"He goes forth over the family of Mikhlaq with a bowl, like the cistern of the Iraqi elder, overflowing."

Ibn Hamid? No—here is the translation.

Abu Bakr al-Hamshawi informed us, saying: Abu Bakr al-Qati'i Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah ibn Muslim informed me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Sahl al-Sarraj narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Hasan say: (wa-jifanin ka-l-jawab) "like the watering troughs of camels." It is said that a thousand men would gather around one single bowl, eating before him.

Wa-qudurin rasiyat: fixed in place, not moved or shifted from their positions because of their enormity, and not taken down or left unused. They were in Yemen, and from the same root comes the term for mountains, rawasi (firmly fixed ones).

I'malu aal Dawud shukran: that is, "We said: Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude," meaning: work in obedience to God, O family of Dawud, in thanks for His blessings. Shukran is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar).

Wa-qalilun min ibadiya al-shakur: Hamzah read it with a sukun on the ya' (yā’), and the rest read it with a fatha. Al-Qurazi said: gratitude (shukr) is fear of God and acting in obedience to Him.

They also narrated to us on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, saying: al-Hasr ibn Aban narrated to us, saying: Sayyar narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Thabit say: Dawud, the Prophet of God (peace be upon him), had divided the hours of the night and day among his family, so that at no hour of the night or day was there not someone from the family of Dawud standing in prayer. Thus God included them all in this verse: I'malu aal Dawud shukran.

Fa-lamma qadayna alayhi al-mawt: The exegetes said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) would seclude himself in Bayt al-Maqdis for a year, two years, a month, two months, or less or more, and his food and drink would be brought in to him. He entered it on the occasion in which he died. The sign of this was that every morning a tree would sprout in Bayt al-Maqdis, and he would ask it: "What is your name?" The tree would say: "My name is such-and-such." He would say: "For what purpose are you?" It would say: "For such-and-such." Then he would order it cut down. If it had sprouted for planting, he would plant it; if it was for medicine, it would be recorded.

Then one day, while he was praying, he saw a tree before him, and he said to it: "What is your name?" It said: "Al-Kharrubah (the carob)." He said: "For what purpose did you sprout?" It said: "For the ruin of this mosque." Sulayman said: "God would not ruin it while I am alive. You are the one on whose account my death and the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis will come." He uprooted it, planted it in a courtyard of his, then said: "O God, conceal my death from the jinn, so that mankind will know that the jinn do not know the unseen," for the jinn used to tell mankind that they knew some of the unseen and what would happen tomorrow. Then he entered the prayer niche (mihrab) and stood praying, leaning on his staff, and he died.

Ibn Zayd said: Sulayman said to the Angel of Death: "When you are commanded concerning me, inform me." So he came to him and said: "O Sulayman, I have been commanded concerning you, and only a short while remains for you."

He summoned the devils, and they built around him a palace of glass with no door. He stood praying, leaning on his staff, and the Angel of Death entered upon him and seized his soul while he was leaning on his staff.

In another narration: Sulayman (peace be upon him) said one day to his companions: "God has given me the kingdom that you see, and no day has passed over me in my rule in which it was clear of turbidity. I have wished that I might have one day that is clear for me until night, in which I am not grieved; but that day is tomorrow."

When the next day came, he entered one of his palaces and ordered its doors to be closed, and prevented people from entering upon him, and kept news from reaching him, lest he hear anything on that day that would distress him. Then he took his staff in hand, climbed to the top of his palace, and leaned on his staff, looking over his kingdoms. Suddenly he saw a young man of handsome face, wearing white garments, who had come upon him from one side of his palace. He said: "Peace be upon you, O Sulayman." He said: "And upon you peace. How did you enter this palace, when you were forbidden to enter it? Did the gatekeeper and the chamberlains not prevent you? Did you not stand in awe of me when you entered my palace without my permission?" He said: "I am one whom no chamberlain can hold back, and no doorkeeper can repel, and I do not fear kings, nor do I accept bribes, and I would not have entered this palace without permission." Sulayman said: "Who gave you permission to enter it?" He said: "Its Lord."

Sulayman trembled and knew that he was the Angel of Death. He said to him: "Are you the Angel of Death?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then for what have you come?" He said: "I have come to seize your soul." He said: "O Angel of Death, this is a day I wished would be clear for me, and that I would not hear in it anything that grieves me." He said: "O Sulayman, you wished for a day in which your life would be clear and in which you would not be grieved. That day has not been created among the days of this world. So be content with the decree of your Lord, for it has no reversal."

He said: "Then carry out what you were commanded."

The Angel of Death seized his soul while he was leaning on his staff. They said: the devils used to gather around his prayer niche and place of prayer wherever he was. The prayer niche had openings (kuwwa) before him and behind him, and a devil who wanted to leave would say: "Am I not bold enough? If I enter and exit from that side..." and he would enter and exit from the other side. One of those devils entered, passed through, and did not hear Sulayman's voice; then he returned and did not hear it; then he returned and fell into the room, but was not burned. He looked at Sulayman, who had fallen dead. So he went out and informed the people that Sulayman had died. They opened the place for him and brought him out, and they found his staff, which in the Abyssinian tongue is "minsa'ah," eaten by termites. They did not know how long he had been dead, so they placed termites on the staff, and it was eaten by them for a day and a night. Then they calculated accordingly and found that he had been dead for a year. The jinn had been working before him, looking at him and thinking he was alive, and they did not notice his absence from going out to the people because of his long prayer before that. [Tafsir al-Tabari 22/92; Tarikh al-Tabari 1/356.]

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "They continued toiling for him a full year after his death." The people then realized that the jinn had been lying to them, and that if they had known the unseen they would have known of Sulayman's death and would not have remained in humiliating torment, working for him for a year. Then the devils said to the termite: "If you ate food, we would bring you the finest food, and if you drank drink, we would give you the finest drink, but we will transport mud and water to you." So they carried these to it wherever it was. He said: Have you not seen the mud that is on wood? It is from what the devils bring to it, out of gratitude to it. This is the meaning of God's words: Fa-lamma qadayna alayhi al-mawt ma dallahum ala mawtihi illa dabbat al-ard, which is the termite. It is also called al-qadih, and it is a small creature that eats wood.

Ta'kulu minsa'atahu: that is, his staff. Its root is from "nasa'a al-ghanam," when one drives and herds the sheep. Tarafah said:

"Strong, like boards of Aran wood, I drove her on a road like the back of a striped cloak."

That is, I drove her. Most readers pronounce the hamza, while Abu Amr and the people of Medina leave it unpronounced, and both are dialects. A poet who used the hamza said:

"We struck with a staff his face, so he became humiliated and abased thereby."

Others, who left out the hamza, said:

"If you walk upon the staff in old age, then idle talk and dalliance have departed far from you."

His words: Fa-lamma kharra tabayyanat al-jinnu an law kanu ya'lamuna al-ghayba ma labithu fi al-adhab al-muhin. The "an" is in the nominative position, because the meaning is: when he fell, it became clear and was revealed that, had the jinn... i.e., their situation became manifest. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "an law kana al-jinnu yalamuna al-ghayba ma labithu fi al-adhab al-muhin." It is also said that "an" is in the accusative position, meaning: the jinn knew and were certain that, had they known the unseen...

The historians said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) lived fifty-three years, and his reign lasted forty years. He became king at the age of thirteen, and he began building Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 34, verse 12–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind" (al-rih). The common reading is with a fatha on the ḥā' (al-rīḥa), meaning: "And We subjected the wind to Sulayman." Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal related from ʿĀṣim a reading with a ḍammah (al-rīḥu), on the basis of the preposition of accompaniment being understood (the phrase being in the nominative, with the sense of "and for Sulayman was the wind").

"Its morning course is a month, and its evening course is a month": from midday until night is a month's journey. [Mā] [[An addition required by the context.]] So it carries him in a single day over the distance of two months' journey.

Wahb said: It was mentioned to me that on a dwelling in the region of the Tigris there was written an inscription [written] [[In the manuscript: kataba-hu.]] by one of the companions of Sulayman (peace be upon him), whether from among the jinn or from among mankind: "By a sea we descended, and we did not build it; built, we found it. We set out in the morning from Istakhr and we said, and we are returning from it, God willing, and will spend the night in Syria."

al-Hasan said: When the horses occupied Prophet Sulayman son of Dawud to the point that he missed the ʿAṣr prayer, he became angry for God's sake and slaughtered (ʿaqara) the horses. God the Exalted replaced them for him with something better and quicker: they run at his command however he wills, "its morning course is a month and its evening course is a month." He would set out from Iliya, take a midday rest at Istakhr, then depart from there and arrive in the evening at Kabul.

Ibn Zayd said: He (peace be upon him) had a vessel of wood, and in it were a thousand pillars, and at each pillar a thousand chambers; with him there rode in it men from the jinn and mankind, and beneath each pillar a thousand devils who lifted that vessel. When it rose, the gentle wind came and carried it along with them. He would take his midday rest among a people with a month's distance between him and them, and his evening rest among another people with a month's distance between him and them, so the people would not know until the armies had overshadowed them.

It is related that Sulayman (peace be upon him) journeyed from the land of Iraq in the morning and stopped at the city of Marw, and prayed ʿAṣr in the city of Balkh, carried by the wind with his soldiers, and the birds shading them. Then he travelled from the city of Balkh, passing through the lands of the Turks, then passed beyond them to the land of China, going out in the morning a month's distance and returning in the evening a similar distance. Then he turned to the right from the rising of the sun along the seashore until he reached the land of Qandahar, and went out from it to Makran and Kirman, then passed beyond them until he reached the land of Persia and stayed there some days, and set out in the morning and stopped at Kaskar, then returned to Syria, and his residence was in the city of Tadmur. The devils had, before his departure from Syria to Iraq, been ordered by him to build it, so they built it for him with slabs of stone, columns, and white and yellow marble. Concerning that, al-Nabigha says:

"Behold Sulayman, when the God said to him: 'Rise up in the wilderness and clear it of the ...'
And subdue the jinn, for I have permitted them: they build Tadmur with slabs and columns."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 13/121 and Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 14/269.]]

I found these verses carved on a rock in the land of Kaskar, composed by one of the companions of Sulayman son of Dawud (peace be upon them both):

"We, and there is no might save the might of our Lord, return to our homelands from the land of Tadmur.
When we return, the time of our rest is a month's journey, and the morning of the next [is a month's journey].
People who sold their souls to God willingly, for the victory of the son of Dawud, the purified Prophet.
For them is virtue and elevation in the lofty matters of religion, and if they are ever traced, they are of the best of tribes.
Whenever they mount the obedient wind, it hastens, swift, not falling short of its month.
Birds in ranks shade them; whenever they flutter above them, they do not startle."

His saying: "And We caused the spring of copper to flow for him" (ʿayn al-qiṭr): We melted for him the copper ore, which flowed for him for three days as water flows. It was in the land of Yemen, and people benefit today from what God brought forth for Sulayman.

"And whoever deviates" (yazigh): turns away and swerves "from Our command" which We commanded him, of obedience to Sulayman, "We shall make him taste the punishment of the blaze" (al-saʿir) in the Hereafter. This is the view of most exegetes, while some said it is in this world: God the Exalted had appointed over them an angel holding a whip of fire, so whoever deviated from the command of Sulayman, he struck with a blow that burned him.

"They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries" (maḥārīb): places of worship, dwellings, and palaces. The maḥrāb is the front of every masjid, and a majlis (assembly) and a house. ʿAdi said:

"Like dolls of ivory in the sanctuaries, or like eggs in the meadow, its flower [shining] [[So in the sources of the tafsir, see Tafsir al-Tabari; it is the correct metre; in the manuscript: mustakbir.]]"

Among what they made for him of that was the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Its story and description, as mentioned by the people of expertise in histories, is that God the Exalted blessed the progeny of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) until He made them numerous beyond counting. When the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) came, he remained among them thirty years in the land of Palestine, and they increased in number every day, so Dawud was pleased by their multitude and ordered them counted. They kept counting for a period of time until they despaired and were unable to encompass the number of the Children of Israel. God revealed to Dawud: "I had promised your father Ibrahim on the day I commanded him to slaughter his son that he would be truthful to Me and carry out My command, and that I would bless his offspring until they become more than the number of the stars of the heaven and until those who count cannot enumerate them. I have sworn to test them with a calamity by which their number will diminish and your pride in their multitude will depart from you." He gave him the choice between punishing them with hunger and famine for three years, or letting their enemy overpower them for three months, or sending the plague upon them for three days.

Dawud gathered the Children of Israel and informed them of what God had revealed to him and of the choice given to him in it. They said: "You know best what is easier for us, and you are our prophet, so decide for us. Only, we have no patience with hunger, and the enemy's domination is a disgraceful matter; if it must be, then death." So Dawud (peace be upon him) commanded them to prepare themselves for death, so they washed, perfumed themselves, put on shrouds, and went out to the open ground with their children and families, and he ordered them to cry out to God and beseech Him, perhaps [[In the manuscript there is an addition: "that"]] He would have mercy on them. That was in the open ground of Bayt al-Maqdis before the building of the mosque.

He said: Dawud (peace be upon him) ascended above the rock, then fell down prostrating, supplicating to God the Exalted, and God sent the plague upon them. In one day and night it destroyed of them such a number that they were not free from burying them until after a period of two months. When they awoke on the second day, Dawud prostrated and they prostrated with him until the sun rose, and they did not lift their heads until God lifted the plague from them.

They said: When God the Exalted interceded for the Children of Israel through Dawud at that place, Dawud gathered the Children of Israel after three days and said to them: "God the Holy has bestowed grace upon you and shown you mercy, so renew your thanks to Him." They said: "How do you command us?" He said: "I command you to take from this open ground, upon which He has shown you mercy, a mosque in which there will always remain from you and from those after you one who remembers."

When they intended to build, a righteous poor man came to test them, to know how sincere they were in their steadfastness. He said to the Children of Israel: "I have a place in it that I need, and it is not lawful for you to keep me from it." They said to him: "O man, there is no one among the Children of Israel who does not have in this open ground a right like your right, so do not be the most miserly of people nor constrict us in it." He said: "I do not know my right, and you do not know it." They said to him: "Either you be content and be at ease in soul, or we will take it from you by force." He said to them: "Or do you find that in the judgment of God and in the judgment of Dawud?"

He said: They raised his report to Dawud, and he said: "Satisfy him." They said: "For how much shall we take it, O Prophet of God?" He said: "Take it for a hundred sheep." The man said: "Add." Dawud said: "For a hundred cows." He said: "Add." He said: "A hundred camels." He said: "Add to me, for what you are buying is for God the Exalted." Dawud said: "As for when you say this, then name your price and I will give it to you." He said: "Buy from me an orchard like it, of olives, date palms and grapes." He said: "Yes." He said: "Buy it for God, and do not be stingy." He said: "Ask what you will and I will give it to you, or if you wish I will hire myself out to you." He said: "And would you do that, O Prophet of God?" He said: "Yes, if you wish." He said:

"You are more honoured before God than that. Rather, build around it a high wall and fill it with gold, or silver if you wish."

Dawud said: "It is easy."

Then the man turned to the Children of Israel and said: "This is the sincere repentant." Then he said to Dawud: "O Prophet of God, that God should forgive me one sin is dearer to me than everything He has given me, but I was testing you."

So they set about building Bayt al-Maqdis, and Dawud (peace be upon him) would carry the stones for them upon his shoulder, as did the best of the Children of Israel, until they raised it to the height of a man. Then God the Exalted revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him): "This is a holy house, and you are a man who sheds blood a great deal, so you shall not build it unless I decree that by your hand. But a son of yours who will reign after you, named Sulayman, I will make him free of shedding blood, and I will decree its completion by his hand; and that will be his fame and his remembrance for you, lasting."

They prayed in it for a time, and Dawud was then a son of one hundred and twenty-seven years. When he reached the age of one hundred and forty years, God took him, and Sulayman succeeded him. He loved building Bayt al-Maqdis, so he gathered the jinn and the devils and divided the labours among them, assigning each group to a task suited to it. He sent the jinn and the devils to obtain marble and pure white al-mahā from their mines, and commanded that the city be built with marble and slabs. He made it twelve quarters (arbād), and settled in each quarter one of the tribes, and they were twelve tribes.

When he finished building the city, he began building the mosque. He directed the devils in groups: some extracting gold, silver and rubies from their mines and pure pearls from the sea; some tearing out jewels and stones from their places; and some bringing musk and ambergris. Of that there came a quantity that none can count but God the Exalted. Then he summoned the craftsmen and ordered them to cut those raised stones and shape them into slabs, and to prepare those jewels and drill the rubies and pearls. They were working on them, and they made a loud sound because of their hardness, and Sulayman disliked those sounds. He called the jinn and said to them: "Do you have a device for cutting these jewels without noise?"

They said: "O Messenger of God, there is none among the jinn with more experience nor more knowledge than Sakhr al-ʿIfrit. Send for him and he will bring it to you." So Sulayman sealed his ring with a seal (he used to seal the devils with copper and the rest of the jinn with iron), and whenever he sealed one of them with his ring, it shone like a flashing lightning, so no one saw it:

"No jinn nor devil but yielded to him, by the permission of God, mighty is His power."

He sent the seal with ten of the jinn, and they came to him while he was on some island in the seas. They showed him the seal, and when he looked at it he nearly fainted from fear; so he came hastening with the messengers until he entered upon Sulayman (peace be upon him). Sulayman asked his messengers what the ifrit had done on his way. They said: "O Messenger of God, he used to laugh at some of the people at times." Sulayman (peace be upon him) said to him: "Were you not content with your rebellion against me, in not coming to me in obedience, until you began to mock people?"

He said: "O Prophet of God, I did not mock them, except that my laughter was out of wonder at what I heard and saw on my way." Sulayman said: "And what was that?"

He said: "Know that I passed by a man on the bank of a river, with a mule that he wished to water, and with him a jug with which he wished to draw water. He watered the mule and filled the jug, then he wanted to relieve himself, so he tied the mule by the handle of the jug; the mule bolted and dragged the jug and broke it. I laughed at the folly of the man, for he imagined that the jug would hold back the mule.

"And I passed by a man sitting beside a cobbler whom he hired to repair a shoe of his; I heard him stipulate with him that he repair it so that it would last four years, and he forgot that death might come upon him before that. I laughed at his heedlessness and ignorance.

"And I passed by an old woman who was soothsaying and telling people what they did not know of the affairs of the heavens, and I had known that a man had buried a great deal of gold in the place of her bed in past ages. I saw her dying of hunger while under her bed was much gold, of whose place she did not know; then she tells people about the affairs of the heavens, so I laughed at her.

"And I passed by a man in some town, who had an illness, it is said, and he ate onions and was cured of his illness, and he began to practise medicine for people; whoever came to him asking about an ailment, he commanded him to eat onions, and they are the most harmful of things, to the point that their harm reaches the brain. So I laughed at him.

"And I passed by some markets, and I saw garlic, which is the best of all remedies, being sold by measure, and I saw pepper, which is one of the deadly poisons, being sold by weight; so I laughed at that.

"And I passed by people who had sat supplicating God the Exalted and asking Him for forgiveness and mercy; some of them grew weary and got up, and others came and sat, and I saw mercy descend upon them. The mercy missed those who were of the original assembly and overtook those who came and sat; so I laughed in wonder at the decree and the destiny."

They said: Sulayman said to him: "Have you, in your great experience and your wanderings on land and sea, known of anything with which these jewels can be cut, so that it softens and their cutting and drilling become easy without noise?" He said: "Yes, O Prophet of God, I know a white stone like milk called al-samur, but I do not know the mine in which it is found; and among birds there is nothing more clever nor more guided than the eagle. Order an eagle to have its chicks placed in a box of stone with it for a night; then release that eagle and leave its chicks in the box, and it will certainly bring that stone and strike with it the back of the box until it breaks through, so as to reach its chicks."
