He said: Sulayman commanded an eagle with its chicks; he placed it in a box of stone for a day and a night, then released the eagle without the chicks. The eagle went off and came back with that stone after a day and a night, and broke the box with it until it reached its chicks. Sulayman sent with the eagle a band of the jinn until they brought him from it an amount that he knew was sufficient, and he used that for the craftsmen's tools, so that cutting became easy for them without noise. It is the stone used to engrave rings and drill jewels to this day, and it is a rare and precious stone.

He said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) built the mosque with white, yellow and green marble, and supported it with columns of pure al-mahā, and roofed it with slabs of precious jewels, and inlaid its ceilings and walls with pearls, rubies and all kinds of jewels, and paved its floor with slabs of turquoise. There was not on earth at that time a house more splendid or brighter than that mosque; it shone in the darkness like the moon on the night of the full moon.

When he finished it, he gathered to him the best of the Children of Israel and informed them that he had built it for God, and that everything in it was purely for God; and he made the day on which he finished it a festival.

They also said: Among the wonders that Sulayman (peace be upon him) made in Bayt al-Maqdis is that he built a house and plastered its wall with green clay and polished it; whenever a pious, righteous person entered it, his image appeared white on that wall, and whenever a wicked, dissolute person entered, his image appeared black on it. Many people then refrained from immorality and treachery.

In one corner of the mosque he set up a staff of ebony; whoever touched it of the sons of the prophets, its touch did not harm him, and whoever touched it of others, his hand burned.

Al-Awza'i related from Rabi'ah ibn Yazid from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Daylami from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When Sulayman finished building Bayt al-Maqdis, he asked his Lord for three things, and He gave him two, and I hope that God has given him the third: he asked for a judgment that would coincide with His judgment, and He gave it to him; he asked for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, and He gave it to him; and he asked that no one who comes to this house and prays two rak'ahs in it would leave his sins behind, like the day his mother bore him, and I hope that He has given him that." [31] [[Al-Mustadrak: 2/434, with slight variation.]]

They said: Bayt al-Maqdis remained as Sulayman (peace be upon him) built it, until Nebuchadnezzar invaded, destroyed the city and demolished it, dismantled the mosque, and took what was in its ceilings and walls of gold, silver, pearls, rubies and all kinds of jewels, and carried it with him to the seat of his kingdom in the land of Iraq.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: When Sulayman finished building Bayt al-Maqdis, its doors were locked; Sulayman tried them but they would not open, until in his supplication he said: "By the prayers of Abu Dawud, open the doors!" So they opened. Sulayman appointed for it ten thousand of the Qur'an-reciters of the Children of Israel: five thousand by night and five thousand by day, so that no hour of night or day passed without God being worshipped in it.

Tamathil (images) means pictures; they made images in the mosques of copper, brass, tin, glass and marble, images of angels and righteous prophets, so that when people saw them depicted they would worship as they worshipped.

Jifan (basins) means bowls, their singular being jafnah. Kal-jawab (like cisterns) means like the reservoirs into which water is gathered, that is, collected; its singular is jabiyah.

al-Acsha Maymun ibn Qays said:

"He goes forth over the family of Mikhlaq with a bowl, like the cistern of the Iraqi elder, overflowing."

Ibn Hamid? No—here is the translation.

Abu Bakr al-Hamshawi informed us, saying: Abu Bakr al-Qati'i Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah ibn Muslim informed me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Sahl al-Sarraj narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Hasan say: (wa-jifanin ka-l-jawab) "like the watering troughs of camels." It is said that a thousand men would gather around one single bowl, eating before him.

Wa-qudurin rasiyat: fixed in place, not moved or shifted from their positions because of their enormity, and not taken down or left unused. They were in Yemen, and from the same root comes the term for mountains, rawasi (firmly fixed ones).

I'malu aal Dawud shukran: that is, "We said: Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude," meaning: work in obedience to God, O family of Dawud, in thanks for His blessings. Shukran is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar).

Wa-qalilun min ibadiya al-shakur: Hamzah read it with a sukun on the ya' (yā’), and the rest read it with a fatha. Al-Qurazi said: gratitude (shukr) is fear of God and acting in obedience to Him.

They also narrated to us on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, saying: al-Hasr ibn Aban narrated to us, saying: Sayyar narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Thabit say: Dawud, the Prophet of God (peace be upon him), had divided the hours of the night and day among his family, so that at no hour of the night or day was there not someone from the family of Dawud standing in prayer. Thus God included them all in this verse: I'malu aal Dawud shukran.

Fa-lamma qadayna alayhi al-mawt: The exegetes said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) would seclude himself in Bayt al-Maqdis for a year, two years, a month, two months, or less or more, and his food and drink would be brought in to him. He entered it on the occasion in which he died. The sign of this was that every morning a tree would sprout in Bayt al-Maqdis, and he would ask it: "What is your name?" The tree would say: "My name is such-and-such." He would say: "For what purpose are you?" It would say: "For such-and-such." Then he would order it cut down. If it had sprouted for planting, he would plant it; if it was for medicine, it would be recorded.

Then one day, while he was praying, he saw a tree before him, and he said to it: "What is your name?" It said: "Al-Kharrubah (the carob)." He said: "For what purpose did you sprout?" It said: "For the ruin of this mosque." Sulayman said: "God would not ruin it while I am alive. You are the one on whose account my death and the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis will come." He uprooted it, planted it in a courtyard of his, then said: "O God, conceal my death from the jinn, so that mankind will know that the jinn do not know the unseen," for the jinn used to tell mankind that they knew some of the unseen and what would happen tomorrow. Then he entered the prayer niche (mihrab) and stood praying, leaning on his staff, and he died.

Ibn Zayd said: Sulayman said to the Angel of Death: "When you are commanded concerning me, inform me." So he came to him and said: "O Sulayman, I have been commanded concerning you, and only a short while remains for you."

He summoned the devils, and they built around him a palace of glass with no door. He stood praying, leaning on his staff, and the Angel of Death entered upon him and seized his soul while he was leaning on his staff.

In another narration: Sulayman (peace be upon him) said one day to his companions: "God has given me the kingdom that you see, and no day has passed over me in my rule in which it was clear of turbidity. I have wished that I might have one day that is clear for me until night, in which I am not grieved; but that day is tomorrow."

When the next day came, he entered one of his palaces and ordered its doors to be closed, and prevented people from entering upon him, and kept news from reaching him, lest he hear anything on that day that would distress him. Then he took his staff in hand, climbed to the top of his palace, and leaned on his staff, looking over his kingdoms. Suddenly he saw a young man of handsome face, wearing white garments, who had come upon him from one side of his palace. He said: "Peace be upon you, O Sulayman." He said: "And upon you peace. How did you enter this palace, when you were forbidden to enter it? Did the gatekeeper and the chamberlains not prevent you? Did you not stand in awe of me when you entered my palace without my permission?" He said: "I am one whom no chamberlain can hold back, and no doorkeeper can repel, and I do not fear kings, nor do I accept bribes, and I would not have entered this palace without permission." Sulayman said: "Who gave you permission to enter it?" He said: "Its Lord."

Sulayman trembled and knew that he was the Angel of Death. He said to him: "Are you the Angel of Death?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then for what have you come?" He said: "I have come to seize your soul." He said: "O Angel of Death, this is a day I wished would be clear for me, and that I would not hear in it anything that grieves me." He said: "O Sulayman, you wished for a day in which your life would be clear and in which you would not be grieved. That day has not been created among the days of this world. So be content with the decree of your Lord, for it has no reversal."

He said: "Then carry out what you were commanded."

The Angel of Death seized his soul while he was leaning on his staff. They said: the devils used to gather around his prayer niche and place of prayer wherever he was. The prayer niche had openings (kuwwa) before him and behind him, and a devil who wanted to leave would say: "Am I not bold enough? If I enter and exit from that side..." and he would enter and exit from the other side. One of those devils entered, passed through, and did not hear Sulayman's voice; then he returned and did not hear it; then he returned and fell into the room, but was not burned. He looked at Sulayman, who had fallen dead. So he went out and informed the people that Sulayman had died. They opened the place for him and brought him out, and they found his staff, which in the Abyssinian tongue is "minsa'ah," eaten by termites. They did not know how long he had been dead, so they placed termites on the staff, and it was eaten by them for a day and a night. Then they calculated accordingly and found that he had been dead for a year. The jinn had been working before him, looking at him and thinking he was alive, and they did not notice his absence from going out to the people because of his long prayer before that. [Tafsir al-Tabari 22/92; Tarikh al-Tabari 1/356.]

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "They continued toiling for him a full year after his death." The people then realized that the jinn had been lying to them, and that if they had known the unseen they would have known of Sulayman's death and would not have remained in humiliating torment, working for him for a year. Then the devils said to the termite: "If you ate food, we would bring you the finest food, and if you drank drink, we would give you the finest drink, but we will transport mud and water to you." So they carried these to it wherever it was. He said: Have you not seen the mud that is on wood? It is from what the devils bring to it, out of gratitude to it. This is the meaning of God's words: Fa-lamma qadayna alayhi al-mawt ma dallahum ala mawtihi illa dabbat al-ard, which is the termite. It is also called al-qadih, and it is a small creature that eats wood.

Ta'kulu minsa'atahu: that is, his staff. Its root is from "nasa'a al-ghanam," when one drives and herds the sheep. Tarafah said:

"Strong, like boards of Aran wood, I drove her on a road like the back of a striped cloak."

That is, I drove her. Most readers pronounce the hamza, while Abu Amr and the people of Medina leave it unpronounced, and both are dialects. A poet who used the hamza said:

"We struck with a staff his face, so he became humiliated and abased thereby."

Others, who left out the hamza, said:

"If you walk upon the staff in old age, then idle talk and dalliance have departed far from you."

His words: Fa-lamma kharra tabayyanat al-jinnu an law kanu ya'lamuna al-ghayba ma labithu fi al-adhab al-muhin. The "an" is in the nominative position, because the meaning is: when he fell, it became clear and was revealed that, had the jinn... i.e., their situation became manifest. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "an law kana al-jinnu yalamuna al-ghayba ma labithu fi al-adhab al-muhin." It is also said that "an" is in the accusative position, meaning: the jinn knew and were certain that, had they known the unseen...

The historians said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) lived fifty-three years, and his reign lasted forty years. He became king at the age of thirteen, and he began building Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 34, verses 15–27 (part 1 of 2)**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba﴾.

Abu Sabra al-Nakha'i narrated from Farwa ibn Musayk al-Ghatifi, who said:

A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Sheba: was it a man, a woman, a land, a mountain, or a valley?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It was neither a land nor a woman, but it was a man from the Arabs who had ten sons. Six of them went to the right (tayammun) and four went to the left (tasha'um). As for those who went to the right: Kinda, the Ash'ariyyun, al-Azd, Madhhij, Anmar, and Himyar."

A man said: "And what is Anmar?" He said: "Those from whom are Khath'am and Bajila. As for those who went to the left: 'Amila, Judham, Lakhm, and Ghassan."[32][[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 22/94; Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/539, with some alteration of the order in the hadith.]]

The declension and the non-declension of the name are both permissible, and both have been read. Declension treats it as the name of a known man; non-declension treats it as the name of a tribe, like ﴿this is Tamim﴾. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, citing the verse ﴿in their dwellings﴾ (مساكنهم).

The readers differed concerning it. Hamza and al-Nakha'i read ﴿مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾ (maskanihim) with a fatha on the kaf, in the singular. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the kaf, in the singular. The rest read ﴿مساكنهم﴾ (masakinahum) in the plural.

﴿A sign﴾: a proof of Our oneness and Our power. Then He explained it, saying: ﴿two gardens﴾, meaning: they were two gardens, two orchards, ﴿on the right and on the left﴾, for whoever came to them, and on his left. ﴿Eat﴾: it was said to them, ﴿eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him﴾ for what He has bestowed upon you. Here the speech ends, and then it begins anew, saying: ﴿a good land﴾, meaning: this is a land, or your land is a good land, not salty (sabakha). Ibn Zayd said: "No gnat, fly, flea, scorpion, or snake was ever seen in their land. Caravans would come with lice and vermin in their clothes, and as soon as they looked at their houses the vermin would die. A man would enter the two gardens carrying a basket (qifa) on his head, and when he came out it would be full of all kinds of fruit, though he had not touched any of it with his hand." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿a good land﴾ in its air, ﴿and a Lord Forgiving﴾ of error, ﴿abundant in bounty﴾.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But they turned away﴾. Wahb said: "Allah sent to Sheba thirteen prophets, who called them to Allah, reminded them of His blessings upon them, and warned them of His punishment. But they denied them and said: 'We know of no blessing of Allah upon us. Let your Lord, whom you claim, withhold this blessing from us if He is able.' This is the meaning of His words: ﴿but they turned away﴾."

﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾. Al-'Arim: the dam and the barrier that holds back water; its singular is 'arima, and its origin is from al-'arama, which is severity and strength.

Ibn 'Abbas, Wahb and others said: "This dam watered their two gardens. It was built, it is said, by Bilqis. When she became queen, her people began to fight over the water of their valley. She tried to forbid them, but they did not obey her. So she abandoned her kingdom and went to one of her palaces and settled there. When the evil among them increased and they regretted it, they came to her and asked her to return to her rule, but she refused. They said: 'You will either return or we will kill you.' She said: 'You do not obey me, and you have no intellect.'

They said: 'We will obey you, for we have found no good among us after you.' So she came and ordered their valley to be dammed with al-'Arim, which is the barrier in the language of Himyar. She blocked the space between the two mountains with rock and pitch, made for it three gates, one above another, and built a huge reservoir behind it. In the reservoir she made twelve outlets, corresponding to the number of their rivers. When the rain came, water gathered behind the dam from the trees and the valleys of Yemen, and the flood was held back behind the dam. She then ordered the upper gate to be opened, and its water flowed into the reservoir. She ordered dung to be cast into it, and some of the dung came out faster than the rest. She kept narrowing those channels and sending dung into the water until they all came out together, and she would divide the water among them in this way. This went on until what happened to her and to Solomon happened."

They remained in this state after her. They used to water from the upper gate, then from the second gate, then from the lowest gate, and the water would never run out until the water returned the following year.

When they transgressed and disbelieved, Allah sent upon them a rat called al-khuld, which dug under the dam from its base. The water drowned their gardens and ruined their land.

Wahb said: "They used to find in their knowledge and their soothsaying, so they claimed, that a mouse would ruin this dam of theirs. So they left no gap between two stones without tying a cat there. When the time came, and Allah willed to scatter them, a red mouse came, so they say, towards one of those cats and attacked it until the cat drew back from it. The mouse entered the gap that had been beside it, crept into the dam, gnawed and dug until it weakened it for the flood, while they did not know. When the flood came it found a weakness and entered it until it uprooted the dam, and it poured over their wealth and drowned it, and the sand buried their houses. They were scattered and dispersed until they became a proverb among the Arabs: 'They scattered like the hands of Sheba' (تفرقوا أيادي سبأ). This is the meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾."

It was also said: al-'Arim is a violent rain, from al-'arama, which is rebelliousness and disobedience.

﴿And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens of bitter fruit (khamt), of tamarisk and of some lote-trees, few.﴾ The common reading is with tanwin (ذواتي أكل خمط). Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with idafa. The two are close in meaning, like the Arab saying: "In the orchard of so-and-so are grapes of a vine (a'nab karm) and grapes of a vine," where sometimes they add the grapes to the vine because they come from it, and sometimes they make the grapes indefinite (with tanwin), and then they describe them by the vine, since grapes are the fruit of the vine.

Al-ukul: the fruit. Al-khamt: according to most exegetes, the arak tree (Salvadora persica). It was said: every thorny tree. It was said: the ghada tree. It was said: any plant that has taken on a bitter taste so that it cannot be eaten. ﴿Wa-athl﴾: the tamarisk, according to Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: a tree resembling the tamarisk but larger than it. Al-Hasan said: al-athl is wood. Qatada said: a kind of wood. It was said: it is the sumr tree. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the nadar tree.

﴿And some lote-trees, few﴾. Qatada said: "While the trees of the people were among the best of trees, Allah turned them into the worst of trees because of their deeds." Al-Kalbi said: "They used to shade themselves under the trees and eat the barbar (a kind of fruit) and the fruit of the lote-tree, but they refused to respond to the messengers."

﴿That We requited them﴾ for what they did, ﴿for their disbelief﴾, meaning: for their unbelief. The place of that is in the accusative, by the occurrence of the requital upon it; its meaning is: ''We requited them that for what they disbelieved.''

﴿And do We requite except the ungrateful?﴾ The people of Kufa read it with a nun and a kasra on the zay and a fatha on the ra' (نجازي... الكفور), and Abu 'Ubayda preferred this, saying: "He said ﴿We requited them﴾ and did not say 'they were requited'." The others read it with a yā' pronounced with a damma, a fatha on the zay and a damma on the ra' (يُجازى... الكفور). The meaning of the verse is: "Is such a recompense given except to the ungrateful?" Mujahid said: yujazi means "yu'aqab", i.e., is punished.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed﴾, which is al-Sham, ﴿towns in view﴾, meaning: connected, the second appearing from the first because of their nearness to it. Al-Hasan said: "One of them would set out in the morning and rest at midday in one town, and in the evening he would lodge in another. A woman would go out with her spindle, and on her head her basket, and she would work with her spindle and not return to her house until her basket was full of fruit. Such was the case between Yemen and al-Sham."

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿towns in view﴾ means Arab towns between Madina and al-Sham. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the towns between Ma'rib and al-Sham. Mujahid said: they are the high plains (al-sarawat). Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they are the towns of San'a'.

﴿And We made travel therein measured﴾, meaning: We made the journey between their towns and the towns We had blessed a measured journey, from station to station and from town to town, so that they would not stop except in a town, nor set out in the morning except in a town. And We said to them: ﴿Travel therein by night and day, safe﴾ whenever you wish, ''you will not fear an enemy, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor will you need provisions or water.'' But they became insolent and transgressed, and they did not endure well-being, and they said: "If the garden of Jinn were farther than these, it would be more fitting for us to desire it."

﴿So they said: "Our Lord, lengthen the distances of our journeys﴾, meaning: make between us and al-Sham deserts and wastelands so that we may ride on mounts and carry provisions. Allah granted them their request. The readers differed concerning this verse. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "Rabbana ba''id" (رَبنا بَعِّد), in the form of supplication and request from al-tabid (making distant), and this is the transmission of Hisham from the readers of al-Sham. Ibn al-Hanafiyya and Ya'qub read: ﴿Rabbu-na﴾ with a damma on the ba', ''ba'ada'' with a fatha on the ba', 'ayn and dal, as a statement; this is the choice of Abu Hatim. They made their journeys distant out of insolence and arrogance. The rest read: ﴿Rabbana﴾ with a fatha on the ba', ''ba'id'' with an alif, a kasra on the 'ayn and a sukun on the dal, as supplication. Allah did that to them."

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief, insolence and transgression. ﴿So We made them tales﴾: a lesson and an example by which they are cited. ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾.

Al-Sha'bi said: "As for Ghassan, they went to al-Sham. As for the Ansar, they went to Yathrib. As for Khuza'a, they went to Tihama. As for al-Azd, they went to 'Uman."

Ibn Ishaq said: "They claim that 'Imran ibn 'Amir, who was the uncle of the people, was a soothsayer, and in his soothsaying he saw that his people would be torn apart and their journeys would be separated. He said to them: 'I know that you will be scattered. So whoever among you has a far-reaching resolve, a heavy burden and a new water-skin, let him join Ka's or Karud.'" He said: "So Wad'a ibn 'Amr went."

"And whoever among you wants a comfortable life and a safe sanctuary, let him join al-Urdunn." So Khuza'a went there. "And whoever among you wants the high-rising ones in the foot and the feeders in times of famine, let him join Yathrib of the palm trees." So al-Aws and al-Khazraj went there. "And whoever among you wants wine, leaven, gold, silk, kingship and command, let him join Kawthaa and Basra." So Ghassan, the sons of Jafna, kings of al-Sham went there, and those of them who were in Iraq.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾ Mutarrif said: "He is the believer who, when he is given, gives thanks, and when he is tested, endures patiently."

The words of Allah: ﴿And certainly did Iblis confirm his assumption about them﴾. The people of Kufa read it with a shadda on the dal, which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, meaning: he made an assumption about them when he said: ﴿So by Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad 38:82], and he said: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf 7:17]. So his assumption was confirmed, and he realized it by their acts toward them and their following him. The others read it with a light dal (صَدَقَ), meaning: his assumption about them was true.

﴿Upon them﴾, meaning: upon the people of Sheba. Mujahid said: upon all people, except those who obey Allah. ﴿And they followed him, except for a party of the believers﴾. ﴿And he had no authority over them except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾: ''except that We gave him power over them, so that We may know,'' meaning: so that We may see and distinguish, and so that We may know him as existing, manifest, and deserving reward and punishment, just as We knew him before as non-existent, after a trial from Us for Our creation.

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he did not strike them with a sword, nor a stick, nor a whip; he only gave them false hopes and deception, to which he called them."

﴿Who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾, the verse.

Say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists among whom you live: ﴿Call those you claimed to be gods besides Allah﴾. Then He described them, saying: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾, of good, evil, harm, or benefit. So how could one who is like that be a god? ﴿And they have no share in them﴾, that is, in the heavens and the earth, ﴿of partnership﴾, a partnership. ﴿And He has not from among them any helper﴾, meaning: any supporter.

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for whom He permits﴾, a denial of them when they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾. Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ''udhina'' (أُذِنَ) with a damma on the alif, and the reading varied from 'Asim. The others read it with a fatha.

﴿Until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the fa' and the zay. The others read it with a damma on the fa' and a kasra on the zay, meaning: the fear is uncovered and removed (أُخرج) from their hearts.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Abu 'Ali ibn Habis the reader informed me, saying: Abu 'Ubayd al-Qadi narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Sabbagh informed me from 'Abd al-Wahhab, from Musa al-Iswari, from al-Hasan, that he used to read it: ﴿until, when fear is removed (فرع) from their hearts﴾ with the ra' and the 'ayn, meaning: their hearts were relieved of fear.

They differed concerning this pronoun, and about those described by this attribute, who they are, and what is the cause for which the fear was removed from their hearts.

One group said: they are the angels. Then they differed about the cause. Some of them said: the fear is removed from their hearts only by a swoon that overtakes them when they hear the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us from Isma'il ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn 'Affan, who said: Ibn Numayr narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, from Masruq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks with the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound like the clanking of a chain on smooth rock, and they swoon and fall prostrate. When they realize that it is revelation, ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾." He said: "Then it is returned to them, and the inhabitants of the heavens call to one another: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ They say: ﴿The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾." Then one of them raised it.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid also informed us, saying: Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'id al-Bazzaz informed me, saying: 'Ali ibn Ashkab narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya informed me, from al-A'mash, from Muslim ibn Subayh, from Masruq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks with the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound in the heaven like the dragging of a chain on a smooth rock, so they swoon and continue in that state until Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them. When Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them, ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾, and they say: 'O Jibril, what has your Lord said?' He says: 'He says: the Truth.' Then they call out: 'The Truth, the Truth.'"[[Fath al-Bari 13/382.]][33]

What supports this hadith and explains it is what:

Abu Muhammad 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Faqih informed us, saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq ibn Ayyub informed me, saying: Bishr ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: al-Humaydi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: I heard 'Ikrima say: I heard Abu Hurayra say: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain on smooth rock. When ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'To the one who said: ﴿the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾.'"[[Sahih al-Bukhari: 6/28.]][34]

'Aqil ibn Muhammad informed me, from al-Mu'afa ibn Zakariyya, from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, from Zakariyya ibn Aban al-Misri, from Nu'aym, from al-Walid ibn Muslim, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, from Abu Zakariyya, from Raja' ibn Haywa, from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "When the people of the heavens hear that, they swoon and fall down prostrate to Allah. The first to raise his head will be Jibril, and Allah will speak to him with His revelation what He wills. Then Jibril passes by the angels; every time he passes a heaven, its angels ask him: 'What has our Lord said, O Jibril?' Jibril says: 'He said the Truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.' He said: They all say the same as what Jibril said. Then Jibril arrives with the revelation at the place where Allah commanded."[[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/94.]][35]

And with this chain, from Ibn Jarir, from Ya'qub, from Ibn 'Ulayya, from Ayyub, from Hisham, from 'Urwa, who said: al-Harith ibn Hisham said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How does the revelation come to you?" He said: "It comes to me like the sound of a bell, and it departs from me when it departs, and I have memorized what it said. And sometimes it comes to me in the form of a man, and he speaks to me, and that is easier for me."[[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 22/111.]][36]

Some of them said: they are startled out of fear of the Hour arriving.

Al-Kalbi said: "Between 'Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them both) there was a long interval, lasting five hundred and fifty years, in which no messengers came. When Allah sent Muhammad (peace be upon him), Allah spoke to Jibril about the message to Muhammad. When the angels heard the sound, they thought the Hour had arrived, and they swooned at what they heard. When Jibril descended, he began to pass by the people of each heaven, and the fear was lifted from them, so they raised their heads, and one of them said to another:"

What did your Lord say? They did not know what He had said, but they replied: "He has said the truth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great." That is because Muhammad, in the eyes of the people of the heavens, was among the signs of the Hour. When God the Exalted sent him, the people of the heavens were terrified, and they had no doubt that it was the Hour.

Al-Dahhak said: The angels "who succeed one another" (al-mu'aqqibat), who go back and forth among the people of the earth and record their deeds, when the Lord sends them down, descend with a loud sound. Those who are below the angels suppose that it is something from the affair of the Hour, so they fall down prostrate and swoon, until they realise that it is not from the affair of the Hour. This is a warning from God, the Glorified, and an informing that the angels, in this state, cannot intercede for anyone except with His permission. When God gives them permission and they hear His revelation, this is their condition. How then could idols intercede?

Others said: Rather, those described by this are the polytheists.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said, meaning: "Until, when the terror is removed from the hearts of the polytheists at the coming of death upon them, as a establishment of proof against them, the angels will say to them: 'What did your Lord say in the world?' They will say: 'The truth.' They acknowledge it when acknowledgment no longer benefits them. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying, at the end of the surah: ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified, and there is no escape﴾ [Saba': 51].

﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: God. And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance, or in clear error.﴾ This is in the manner of fairness in argument, as one who says: "One of us is a liar," while he knows that he himself is truthful and his opponent is a liar.

The meaning is: we and you are not on one matter; one of the two groups is surely guided and the other is astray. The Prophet and those with him are upon guidance, and whoever opposes him is in error. So he denied them in a manner more gentle than an explicit denial.

It has also been said that this is in the manner of mockery toward them, while he was not doubtful of his religion. This is like the saying of the poet, who was Abu al-Aswad:

"The vile ones, the Banu Qushayr, say: 'Do not forget 'Ali all the days.'
They are the paternal cousins of the Prophet and his closest kin; the most beloved of all people to me.
If their love is guidance, then I will attain it; and I am not mistaken if it is error."

He said it without doubt, and he was certain that their love is guidance.

Some of them said: "aw" here means "wa" (and), meaning: "Indeed we are upon guidance, and indeed you, you are in clear error," like the saying of Jarir:

"Are you, Tha'labat al-fawaris, or Riyah, have you equalled them with Tuhayya and al-Khashshab?" [Al-Sihah: 1/120]

meaning: Tha'labah and Riyah.

﴿Say: You will not be asked about what we have committed, and we will not be asked about what you do.﴾ ﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together on the Day of Resurrection, then He will judge between us with truth (yaftahu baynana: He will decide between us), and He is the Judge, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Say: Show me those whom you have joined with Him as partners.﴾ — meaning the idols: "Have they created anything from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens?" Its explanation is in the surahs (al-Malaika) and (al-Ahqaf).

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nay! Rather, He is God, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ He is the Subduer, the Strong, who prevents whom He wills and whom no preventer can prevent. He is the Mighty, the Avenger against those who disbelieve in Him and oppose Him, the Wise in His management of His creation. So how could there be for Him a partner in His dominion?

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 34, verses 15–27 (part 1 of 2)**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba﴾.

Abu Sabra al-Nakha'i narrated from Farwa ibn Musayk al-Ghatifi, who said:

A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Sheba: was it a man, a woman, a land, a mountain, or a valley?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It was neither a land nor a woman, but it was a man from the Arabs who had ten sons. Six of them went to the right (tayammun) and four went to the left (tasha'um). As for those who went to the right: Kinda, the Ash'ariyyun, al-Azd, Madhhij, Anmar, and Himyar."

A man said: "And what is Anmar?" He said: "Those from whom are Khath'am and Bajila. As for those who went to the left: 'Amila, Judham, Lakhm, and Ghassan."[32][[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 22/94; Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/539, with some alteration of the order in the hadith.]]

The declension and the non-declension of the name are both permissible, and both have been read. Declension treats it as the name of a known man; non-declension treats it as the name of a tribe, like ﴿this is Tamim﴾. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, citing the verse ﴿in their dwellings﴾ (مساكنهم).

The readers differed concerning it. Hamza and al-Nakha'i read ﴿مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾ (maskanihim) with a fatha on the kaf, in the singular. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the kaf, in the singular. The rest read ﴿مساكنهم﴾ (masakinahum) in the plural.

﴿A sign﴾: a proof of Our oneness and Our power. Then He explained it, saying: ﴿two gardens﴾, meaning: they were two gardens, two orchards, ﴿on the right and on the left﴾, for whoever came to them, and on his left. ﴿Eat﴾: it was said to them, ﴿eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him﴾ for what He has bestowed upon you. Here the speech ends, and then it begins anew, saying: ﴿a good land﴾, meaning: this is a land, or your land is a good land, not salty (sabakha). Ibn Zayd said: "No gnat, fly, flea, scorpion, or snake was ever seen in their land. Caravans would come with lice and vermin in their clothes, and as soon as they looked at their houses the vermin would die. A man would enter the two gardens carrying a basket (qifa) on his head, and when he came out it would be full of all kinds of fruit, though he had not touched any of it with his hand." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿a good land﴾ in its air, ﴿and a Lord Forgiving﴾ of error, ﴿abundant in bounty﴾.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But they turned away﴾. Wahb said: "Allah sent to Sheba thirteen prophets, who called them to Allah, reminded them of His blessings upon them, and warned them of His punishment. But they denied them and said: 'We know of no blessing of Allah upon us. Let your Lord, whom you claim, withhold this blessing from us if He is able.' This is the meaning of His words: ﴿but they turned away﴾."

﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾. Al-'Arim: the dam and the barrier that holds back water; its singular is 'arima, and its origin is from al-'arama, which is severity and strength.

Ibn 'Abbas, Wahb and others said: "This dam watered their two gardens. It was built, it is said, by Bilqis. When she became queen, her people began to fight over the water of their valley. She tried to forbid them, but they did not obey her. So she abandoned her kingdom and went to one of her palaces and settled there. When the evil among them increased and they regretted it, they came to her and asked her to return to her rule, but she refused. They said: 'You will either return or we will kill you.' She said: 'You do not obey me, and you have no intellect.'

They said: 'We will obey you, for we have found no good among us after you.' So she came and ordered their valley to be dammed with al-'Arim, which is the barrier in the language of Himyar. She blocked the space between the two mountains with rock and pitch, made for it three gates, one above another, and built a huge reservoir behind it. In the reservoir she made twelve outlets, corresponding to the number of their rivers. When the rain came, water gathered behind the dam from the trees and the valleys of Yemen, and the flood was held back behind the dam. She then ordered the upper gate to be opened, and its water flowed into the reservoir. She ordered dung to be cast into it, and some of the dung came out faster than the rest. She kept narrowing those channels and sending dung into the water until they all came out together, and she would divide the water among them in this way. This went on until what happened to her and to Solomon happened."

They remained in this state after her. They used to water from the upper gate, then from the second gate, then from the lowest gate, and the water would never run out until the water returned the following year.

When they transgressed and disbelieved, Allah sent upon them a rat called al-khuld, which dug under the dam from its base. The water drowned their gardens and ruined their land.

Wahb said: "They used to find in their knowledge and their soothsaying, so they claimed, that a mouse would ruin this dam of theirs. So they left no gap between two stones without tying a cat there. When the time came, and Allah willed to scatter them, a red mouse came, so they say, towards one of those cats and attacked it until the cat drew back from it. The mouse entered the gap that had been beside it, crept into the dam, gnawed and dug until it weakened it for the flood, while they did not know. When the flood came it found a weakness and entered it until it uprooted the dam, and it poured over their wealth and drowned it, and the sand buried their houses. They were scattered and dispersed until they became a proverb among the Arabs: 'They scattered like the hands of Sheba' (تفرقوا أيادي سبأ). This is the meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾."

It was also said: al-'Arim is a violent rain, from al-'arama, which is rebelliousness and disobedience.

﴿And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens of bitter fruit (khamt), of tamarisk and of some lote-trees, few.﴾ The common reading is with tanwin (ذواتي أكل خمط). Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with idafa. The two are close in meaning, like the Arab saying: "In the orchard of so-and-so are grapes of a vine (a'nab karm) and grapes of a vine," where sometimes they add the grapes to the vine because they come from it, and sometimes they make the grapes indefinite (with tanwin), and then they describe them by the vine, since grapes are the fruit of the vine.

Al-ukul: the fruit. Al-khamt: according to most exegetes, the arak tree (Salvadora persica). It was said: every thorny tree. It was said: the ghada tree. It was said: any plant that has taken on a bitter taste so that it cannot be eaten. ﴿Wa-athl﴾: the tamarisk, according to Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: a tree resembling the tamarisk but larger than it. Al-Hasan said: al-athl is wood. Qatada said: a kind of wood. It was said: it is the sumr tree. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the nadar tree.

﴿And some lote-trees, few﴾. Qatada said: "While the trees of the people were among the best of trees, Allah turned them into the worst of trees because of their deeds." Al-Kalbi said: "They used to shade themselves under the trees and eat the barbar (a kind of fruit) and the fruit of the lote-tree, but they refused to respond to the messengers."

﴿That We requited them﴾ for what they did, ﴿for their disbelief﴾, meaning: for their unbelief. The place of that is in the accusative, by the occurrence of the requital upon it; its meaning is: ''We requited them that for what they disbelieved.''

﴿And do We requite except the ungrateful?﴾ The people of Kufa read it with a nun and a kasra on the zay and a fatha on the ra' (نجازي... الكفور), and Abu 'Ubayda preferred this, saying: "He said ﴿We requited them﴾ and did not say 'they were requited'." The others read it with a yā' pronounced with a damma, a fatha on the zay and a damma on the ra' (يُجازى... الكفور). The meaning of the verse is: "Is such a recompense given except to the ungrateful?" Mujahid said: yujazi means "yu'aqab", i.e., is punished.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed﴾, which is al-Sham, ﴿towns in view﴾, meaning: connected, the second appearing from the first because of their nearness to it. Al-Hasan said: "One of them would set out in the morning and rest at midday in one town, and in the evening he would lodge in another. A woman would go out with her spindle, and on her head her basket, and she would work with her spindle and not return to her house until her basket was full of fruit. Such was the case between Yemen and al-Sham."

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿towns in view﴾ means Arab towns between Madina and al-Sham. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the towns between Ma'rib and al-Sham. Mujahid said: they are the high plains (al-sarawat). Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they are the towns of San'a'.

﴿And We made travel therein measured﴾, meaning: We made the journey between their towns and the towns We had blessed a measured journey, from station to station and from town to town, so that they would not stop except in a town, nor set out in the morning except in a town. And We said to them: ﴿Travel therein by night and day, safe﴾ whenever you wish, ''you will not fear an enemy, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor will you need provisions or water.'' But they became insolent and transgressed, and they did not endure well-being, and they said: "If the garden of Jinn were farther than these, it would be more fitting for us to desire it."

﴿So they said: "Our Lord, lengthen the distances of our journeys﴾, meaning: make between us and al-Sham deserts and wastelands so that we may ride on mounts and carry provisions. Allah granted them their request. The readers differed concerning this verse. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "Rabbana ba''id" (رَبنا بَعِّد), in the form of supplication and request from al-tabid (making distant), and this is the transmission of Hisham from the readers of al-Sham. Ibn al-Hanafiyya and Ya'qub read: ﴿Rabbu-na﴾ with a damma on the ba', ''ba'ada'' with a fatha on the ba', 'ayn and dal, as a statement; this is the choice of Abu Hatim. They made their journeys distant out of insolence and arrogance. The rest read: ﴿Rabbana﴾ with a fatha on the ba', ''ba'id'' with an alif, a kasra on the 'ayn and a sukun on the dal, as supplication. Allah did that to them."

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief, insolence and transgression. ﴿So We made them tales﴾: a lesson and an example by which they are cited. ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾.

Al-Sha'bi said: "As for Ghassan, they went to al-Sham. As for the Ansar, they went to Yathrib. As for Khuza'a, they went to Tihama. As for al-Azd, they went to 'Uman."

Ibn Ishaq said: "They claim that 'Imran ibn 'Amir, who was the uncle of the people, was a soothsayer, and in his soothsaying he saw that his people would be torn apart and their journeys would be separated. He said to them: 'I know that you will be scattered. So whoever among you has a far-reaching resolve, a heavy burden and a new water-skin, let him join Ka's or Karud.'" He said: "So Wad'a ibn 'Amr went."

"And whoever among you wants a comfortable life and a safe sanctuary, let him join al-Urdunn." So Khuza'a went there. "And whoever among you wants the high-rising ones in the foot and the feeders in times of famine, let him join Yathrib of the palm trees." So al-Aws and al-Khazraj went there. "And whoever among you wants wine, leaven, gold, silk, kingship and command, let him join Kawthaa and Basra." So Ghassan, the sons of Jafna, kings of al-Sham went there, and those of them who were in Iraq.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾ Mutarrif said: "He is the believer who, when he is given, gives thanks, and when he is tested, endures patiently."

The words of Allah: ﴿And certainly did Iblis confirm his assumption about them﴾. The people of Kufa read it with a shadda on the dal, which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, meaning: he made an assumption about them when he said: ﴿So by Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad 38:82], and he said: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf 7:17]. So his assumption was confirmed, and he realized it by their acts toward them and their following him. The others read it with a light dal (صَدَقَ), meaning: his assumption about them was true.

﴿Upon them﴾, meaning: upon the people of Sheba. Mujahid said: upon all people, except those who obey Allah. ﴿And they followed him, except for a party of the believers﴾. ﴿And he had no authority over them except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾: ''except that We gave him power over them, so that We may know,'' meaning: so that We may see and distinguish, and so that We may know him as existing, manifest, and deserving reward and punishment, just as We knew him before as non-existent, after a trial from Us for Our creation.

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he did not strike them with a sword, nor a stick, nor a whip; he only gave them false hopes and deception, to which he called them."

﴿Who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾, the verse.

Say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists among whom you live: ﴿Call those you claimed to be gods besides Allah﴾. Then He described them, saying: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾, of good, evil, harm, or benefit. So how could one who is like that be a god? ﴿And they have no share in them﴾, that is, in the heavens and the earth, ﴿of partnership﴾, a partnership. ﴿And He has not from among them any helper﴾, meaning: any supporter.

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for whom He permits﴾, a denial of them when they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾. Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ''udhina'' (أُذِنَ) with a damma on the alif, and the reading varied from 'Asim. The others read it with a fatha.

﴿Until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the fa' and the zay. The others read it with a damma on the fa' and a kasra on the zay, meaning: the fear is uncovered and removed (أُخرج) from their hearts.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Abu 'Ali ibn Habis the reader informed me, saying: Abu 'Ubayd al-Qadi narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Sabbagh informed me from 'Abd al-Wahhab, from Musa al-Iswari, from al-Hasan, that he used to read it: ﴿until, when fear is removed (فرع) from their hearts﴾ with the ra' and the 'ayn, meaning: their hearts were relieved of fear.

They differed concerning this pronoun, and about those described by this attribute, who they are, and what is the cause for which the fear was removed from their hearts.

One group said: they are the angels. Then they differed about the cause. Some of them said: the fear is removed from their hearts only by a swoon that overtakes them when they hear the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us from Isma'il ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn 'Affan, who said: Ibn Numayr narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, from Masruq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks with the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound like the clanking of a chain on smooth rock, and they swoon and fall prostrate. When they realize that it is revelation, ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾." He said: "Then it is returned to them, and the inhabitants of the heavens call to one another: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ They say: ﴿The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾." Then one of them raised it.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid also informed us, saying: Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'id al-Bazzaz informed me, saying: 'Ali ibn Ashkab narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya informed me, from al-A'mash, from Muslim ibn Subayh, from Masruq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks with the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound in the heaven like the dragging of a chain on a smooth rock, so they swoon and continue in that state until Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them. When Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them, ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾, and they say: 'O Jibril, what has your Lord said?' He says: 'He says: the Truth.' Then they call out: 'The Truth, the Truth.'"[[Fath al-Bari 13/382.]][33]

What supports this hadith and explains it is what:

Abu Muhammad 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Faqih informed us, saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq ibn Ayyub informed me, saying: Bishr ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: al-Humaydi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: I heard 'Ikrima say: I heard Abu Hurayra say: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain on smooth rock. When ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'To the one who said: ﴿the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾.'"[[Sahih al-Bukhari: 6/28.]][34]

'Aqil ibn Muhammad informed me, from al-Mu'afa ibn Zakariyya, from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, from Zakariyya ibn Aban al-Misri, from Nu'aym, from al-Walid ibn Muslim, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, from Abu Zakariyya, from Raja' ibn Haywa, from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "When the people of the heavens hear that, they swoon and fall down prostrate to Allah. The first to raise his head will be Jibril, and Allah will speak to him with His revelation what He wills. Then Jibril passes by the angels; every time he passes a heaven, its angels ask him: 'What has our Lord said, O Jibril?' Jibril says: 'He said the Truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.' He said: They all say the same as what Jibril said. Then Jibril arrives with the revelation at the place where Allah commanded."[[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/94.]][35]

And with this chain, from Ibn Jarir, from Ya'qub, from Ibn 'Ulayya, from Ayyub, from Hisham, from 'Urwa, who said: al-Harith ibn Hisham said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How does the revelation come to you?" He said: "It comes to me like the sound of a bell, and it departs from me when it departs, and I have memorized what it said. And sometimes it comes to me in the form of a man, and he speaks to me, and that is easier for me."[[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 22/111.]][36]

Some of them said: they are startled out of fear of the Hour arriving.

Al-Kalbi said: "Between 'Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them both) there was a long interval, lasting five hundred and fifty years, in which no messengers came. When Allah sent Muhammad (peace be upon him), Allah spoke to Jibril about the message to Muhammad. When the angels heard the sound, they thought the Hour had arrived, and they swooned at what they heard. When Jibril descended, he began to pass by the people of each heaven, and the fear was lifted from them, so they raised their heads, and one of them said to another:"

What did your Lord say? They did not know what He had said, but they replied: "He has said the truth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great." That is because Muhammad, in the eyes of the people of the heavens, was among the signs of the Hour. When God the Exalted sent him, the people of the heavens were terrified, and they had no doubt that it was the Hour.

Al-Dahhak said: The angels "who succeed one another" (al-mu'aqqibat), who go back and forth among the people of the earth and record their deeds, when the Lord sends them down, descend with a loud sound. Those who are below the angels suppose that it is something from the affair of the Hour, so they fall down prostrate and swoon, until they realise that it is not from the affair of the Hour. This is a warning from God, the Glorified, and an informing that the angels, in this state, cannot intercede for anyone except with His permission. When God gives them permission and they hear His revelation, this is their condition. How then could idols intercede?

Others said: Rather, those described by this are the polytheists.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said, meaning: "Until, when the terror is removed from the hearts of the polytheists at the coming of death upon them, as a establishment of proof against them, the angels will say to them: 'What did your Lord say in the world?' They will say: 'The truth.' They acknowledge it when acknowledgment no longer benefits them. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying, at the end of the surah: ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified, and there is no escape﴾ [Saba': 51].

﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: God. And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance, or in clear error.﴾ This is in the manner of fairness in argument, as one who says: "One of us is a liar," while he knows that he himself is truthful and his opponent is a liar.

The meaning is: we and you are not on one matter; one of the two groups is surely guided and the other is astray. The Prophet and those with him are upon guidance, and whoever opposes him is in error. So he denied them in a manner more gentle than an explicit denial.

It has also been said that this is in the manner of mockery toward them, while he was not doubtful of his religion. This is like the saying of the poet, who was Abu al-Aswad:

"The vile ones, the Banu Qushayr, say: 'Do not forget 'Ali all the days.'
They are the paternal cousins of the Prophet and his closest kin; the most beloved of all people to me.
If their love is guidance, then I will attain it; and I am not mistaken if it is error."

He said it without doubt, and he was certain that their love is guidance.

Some of them said: "aw" here means "wa" (and), meaning: "Indeed we are upon guidance, and indeed you, you are in clear error," like the saying of Jarir:

"Are you, Tha'labat al-fawaris, or Riyah, have you equalled them with Tuhayya and al-Khashshab?" [Al-Sihah: 1/120]

meaning: Tha'labah and Riyah.

﴿Say: You will not be asked about what we have committed, and we will not be asked about what you do.﴾ ﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together on the Day of Resurrection, then He will judge between us with truth (yaftahu baynana: He will decide between us), and He is the Judge, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Say: Show me those whom you have joined with Him as partners.﴾ — meaning the idols: "Have they created anything from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens?" Its explanation is in the surahs (al-Malaika) and (al-Ahqaf).

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nay! Rather, He is God, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ He is the Subduer, the Strong, who prevents whom He wills and whom no preventer can prevent. He is the Mighty, the Avenger against those who disbelieve in Him and oppose Him, the Wise in His management of His creation. So how could there be for Him a partner in His dominion?

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 34, verses 15–27 (part 1 of 2)**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba﴾.

Abu Sabra al-Nakha'i narrated from Farwa ibn Musayk al-Ghatifi, who said:

A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Sheba: was it a man, a woman, a land, a mountain, or a valley?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It was neither a land nor a woman, but it was a man from the Arabs who had ten sons. Six of them went to the right (tayammun) and four went to the left (tasha'um). As for those who went to the right: Kinda, the Ash'ariyyun, al-Azd, Madhhij, Anmar, and Himyar."

A man said: "And what is Anmar?" He said: "Those from whom are Khath'am and Bajila. As for those who went to the left: 'Amila, Judham, Lakhm, and Ghassan."[32][[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 22/94; Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/539, with some alteration of the order in the hadith.]]

The declension and the non-declension of the name are both permissible, and both have been read. Declension treats it as the name of a known man; non-declension treats it as the name of a tribe, like ﴿this is Tamim﴾. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, citing the verse ﴿in their dwellings﴾ (مساكنهم).

The readers differed concerning it. Hamza and al-Nakha'i read ﴿مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾ (maskanihim) with a fatha on the kaf, in the singular. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the kaf, in the singular. The rest read ﴿مساكنهم﴾ (masakinahum) in the plural.

﴿A sign﴾: a proof of Our oneness and Our power. Then He explained it, saying: ﴿two gardens﴾, meaning: they were two gardens, two orchards, ﴿on the right and on the left﴾, for whoever came to them, and on his left. ﴿Eat﴾: it was said to them, ﴿eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him﴾ for what He has bestowed upon you. Here the speech ends, and then it begins anew, saying: ﴿a good land﴾, meaning: this is a land, or your land is a good land, not salty (sabakha). Ibn Zayd said: "No gnat, fly, flea, scorpion, or snake was ever seen in their land. Caravans would come with lice and vermin in their clothes, and as soon as they looked at their houses the vermin would die. A man would enter the two gardens carrying a basket (qifa) on his head, and when he came out it would be full of all kinds of fruit, though he had not touched any of it with his hand." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿a good land﴾ in its air, ﴿and a Lord Forgiving﴾ of error, ﴿abundant in bounty﴾.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But they turned away﴾. Wahb said: "Allah sent to Sheba thirteen prophets, who called them to Allah, reminded them of His blessings upon them, and warned them of His punishment. But they denied them and said: 'We know of no blessing of Allah upon us. Let your Lord, whom you claim, withhold this blessing from us if He is able.' This is the meaning of His words: ﴿but they turned away﴾."

﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾. Al-'Arim: the dam and the barrier that holds back water; its singular is 'arima, and its origin is from al-'arama, which is severity and strength.

Ibn 'Abbas, Wahb and others said: "This dam watered their two gardens. It was built, it is said, by Bilqis. When she became queen, her people began to fight over the water of their valley. She tried to forbid them, but they did not obey her. So she abandoned her kingdom and went to one of her palaces and settled there. When the evil among them increased and they regretted it, they came to her and asked her to return to her rule, but she refused. They said: 'You will either return or we will kill you.' She said: 'You do not obey me, and you have no intellect.'

They said: 'We will obey you, for we have found no good among us after you.' So she came and ordered their valley to be dammed with al-'Arim, which is the barrier in the language of Himyar. She blocked the space between the two mountains with rock and pitch, made for it three gates, one above another, and built a huge reservoir behind it. In the reservoir she made twelve outlets, corresponding to the number of their rivers. When the rain came, water gathered behind the dam from the trees and the valleys of Yemen, and the flood was held back behind the dam. She then ordered the upper gate to be opened, and its water flowed into the reservoir. She ordered dung to be cast into it, and some of the dung came out faster than the rest. She kept narrowing those channels and sending dung into the water until they all came out together, and she would divide the water among them in this way. This went on until what happened to her and to Solomon happened."

They remained in this state after her. They used to water from the upper gate, then from the second gate, then from the lowest gate, and the water would never run out until the water returned the following year.

When they transgressed and disbelieved, Allah sent upon them a rat called al-khuld, which dug under the dam from its base. The water drowned their gardens and ruined their land.

Wahb said: "They used to find in their knowledge and their soothsaying, so they claimed, that a mouse would ruin this dam of theirs. So they left no gap between two stones without tying a cat there. When the time came, and Allah willed to scatter them, a red mouse came, so they say, towards one of those cats and attacked it until the cat drew back from it. The mouse entered the gap that had been beside it, crept into the dam, gnawed and dug until it weakened it for the flood, while they did not know. When the flood came it found a weakness and entered it until it uprooted the dam, and it poured over their wealth and drowned it, and the sand buried their houses. They were scattered and dispersed until they became a proverb among the Arabs: 'They scattered like the hands of Sheba' (تفرقوا أيادي سبأ). This is the meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾."

It was also said: al-'Arim is a violent rain, from al-'arama, which is rebelliousness and disobedience.

﴿And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens of bitter fruit (khamt), of tamarisk and of some lote-trees, few.﴾ The common reading is with tanwin (ذواتي أكل خمط). Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with idafa. The two are close in meaning, like the Arab saying: "In the orchard of so-and-so are grapes of a vine (a'nab karm) and grapes of a vine," where sometimes they add the grapes to the vine because they come from it, and sometimes they make the grapes indefinite (with tanwin), and then they describe them by the vine, since grapes are the fruit of the vine.

Al-ukul: the fruit. Al-khamt: according to most exegetes, the arak tree (Salvadora persica). It was said: every thorny tree. It was said: the ghada tree. It was said: any plant that has taken on a bitter taste so that it cannot be eaten. ﴿Wa-athl﴾: the tamarisk, according to Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: a tree resembling the tamarisk but larger than it. Al-Hasan said: al-athl is wood. Qatada said: a kind of wood. It was said: it is the sumr tree. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the nadar tree.

﴿And some lote-trees, few﴾. Qatada said: "While the trees of the people were among the best of trees, Allah turned them into the worst of trees because of their deeds." Al-Kalbi said: "They used to shade themselves under the trees and eat the barbar (a kind of fruit) and the fruit of the lote-tree, but they refused to respond to the messengers."

﴿That We requited them﴾ for what they did, ﴿for their disbelief﴾, meaning: for their unbelief. The place of that is in the accusative, by the occurrence of the requital upon it; its meaning is: ''We requited them that for what they disbelieved.''

﴿And do We requite except the ungrateful?﴾ The people of Kufa read it with a nun and a kasra on the zay and a fatha on the ra' (نجازي... الكفور), and Abu 'Ubayda preferred this, saying: "He said ﴿We requited them﴾ and did not say 'they were requited'." The others read it with a yā' pronounced with a damma, a fatha on the zay and a damma on the ra' (يُجازى... الكفور). The meaning of the verse is: "Is such a recompense given except to the ungrateful?" Mujahid said: yujazi means "yu'aqab", i.e., is punished.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed﴾, which is al-Sham, ﴿towns in view﴾, meaning: connected, the second appearing from the first because of their nearness to it. Al-Hasan said: "One of them would set out in the morning and rest at midday in one town, and in the evening he would lodge in another. A woman would go out with her spindle, and on her head her basket, and she would work with her spindle and not return to her house until her basket was full of fruit. Such was the case between Yemen and al-Sham."

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿towns in view﴾ means Arab towns between Madina and al-Sham. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the towns between Ma'rib and al-Sham. Mujahid said: they are the high plains (al-sarawat). Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they are the towns of San'a'.

﴿And We made travel therein measured﴾, meaning: We made the journey between their towns and the towns We had blessed a measured journey, from station to station and from town to town, so that they would not stop except in a town, nor set out in the morning except in a town. And We said to them: ﴿Travel therein by night and day, safe﴾ whenever you wish, ''you will not fear an enemy, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor will you need provisions or water.'' But they became insolent and transgressed, and they did not endure well-being, and they said: "If the garden of Jinn were farther than these, it would be more fitting for us to desire it."

﴿So they said: "Our Lord, lengthen the distances of our journeys﴾, meaning: make between us and al-Sham deserts and wastelands so that we may ride on mounts and carry provisions. Allah granted them their request. The readers differed concerning this verse. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "Rabbana ba''id" (رَبنا بَعِّد), in the form of supplication and request from al-tabid (making distant), and this is the transmission of Hisham from the readers of al-Sham. Ibn al-Hanafiyya and Ya'qub read: ﴿Rabbu-na﴾ with a damma on the ba', ''ba'ada'' with a fatha on the ba', 'ayn and dal, as a statement; this is the choice of Abu Hatim. They made their journeys distant out of insolence and arrogance. The rest read: ﴿Rabbana﴾ with a fatha on the ba', ''ba'id'' with an alif, a kasra on the 'ayn and a sukun on the dal, as supplication. Allah did that to them."

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief, insolence and transgression. ﴿So We made them tales﴾: a lesson and an example by which they are cited. ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾.

Al-Sha'bi said: "As for Ghassan, they went to al-Sham. As for the Ansar, they went to Yathrib. As for Khuza'a, they went to Tihama. As for al-Azd, they went to 'Uman."

Ibn Ishaq said: "They claim that 'Imran ibn 'Amir, who was the uncle of the people, was a soothsayer, and in his soothsaying he saw that his people would be torn apart and their journeys would be separated. He said to them: 'I know that you will be scattered. So whoever among you has a far-reaching resolve, a heavy burden and a new water-skin, let him join Ka's or Karud.'" He said: "So Wad'a ibn 'Amr went."

"And whoever among you wants a comfortable life and a safe sanctuary, let him join al-Urdunn." So Khuza'a went there. "And whoever among you wants the high-rising ones in the foot and the feeders in times of famine, let him join Yathrib of the palm trees." So al-Aws and al-Khazraj went there. "And whoever among you wants wine, leaven, gold, silk, kingship and command, let him join Kawthaa and Basra." So Ghassan, the sons of Jafna, kings of al-Sham went there, and those of them who were in Iraq.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾ Mutarrif said: "He is the believer who, when he is given, gives thanks, and when he is tested, endures patiently."

The words of Allah: ﴿And certainly did Iblis confirm his assumption about them﴾. The people of Kufa read it with a shadda on the dal, which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, meaning: he made an assumption about them when he said: ﴿So by Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad 38:82], and he said: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf 7:17]. So his assumption was confirmed, and he realized it by their acts toward them and their following him. The others read it with a light dal (صَدَقَ), meaning: his assumption about them was true.

﴿Upon them﴾, meaning: upon the people of Sheba. Mujahid said: upon all people, except those who obey Allah. ﴿And they followed him, except for a party of the believers﴾. ﴿And he had no authority over them except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾: ''except that We gave him power over them, so that We may know,'' meaning: so that We may see and distinguish, and so that We may know him as existing, manifest, and deserving reward and punishment, just as We knew him before as non-existent, after a trial from Us for Our creation.

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he did not strike them with a sword, nor a stick, nor a whip; he only gave them false hopes and deception, to which he called them."

﴿Who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾, the verse.

Say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists among whom you live: ﴿Call those you claimed to be gods besides Allah﴾. Then He described them, saying: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾, of good, evil, harm, or benefit. So how could one who is like that be a god? ﴿And they have no share in them﴾, that is, in the heavens and the earth, ﴿of partnership﴾, a partnership. ﴿And He has not from among them any helper﴾, meaning: any supporter.

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for whom He permits﴾, a denial of them when they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾. Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ''udhina'' (أُذِنَ) with a damma on the alif, and the reading varied from 'Asim. The others read it with a fatha.

﴿Until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the fa' and the zay. The others read it with a damma on the fa' and a kasra on the zay, meaning: the fear is uncovered and removed (أُخرج) from their hearts.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Abu 'Ali ibn Habis the reader informed me, saying: Abu 'Ubayd al-Qadi narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Sabbagh informed me from 'Abd al-Wahhab, from Musa al-Iswari, from al-Hasan, that he used to read it: ﴿until, when fear is removed (فرع) from their hearts﴾ with the ra' and the 'ayn, meaning: their hearts were relieved of fear.

They differed concerning this pronoun, and about those described by this attribute, who they are, and what is the cause for which the fear was removed from their hearts.

One group said: they are the angels. Then they differed about the cause. Some of them said: the fear is removed from their hearts only by a swoon that overtakes them when they hear the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us from Isma'il ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn 'Affan, who said: Ibn Numayr narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, from Masruq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks with the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound like the clanking of a chain on smooth rock, and they swoon and fall prostrate. When they realize that it is revelation, ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾." He said: "Then it is returned to them, and the inhabitants of the heavens call to one another: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ They say: ﴿The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾." Then one of them raised it.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid also informed us, saying: Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'id al-Bazzaz informed me, saying: 'Ali ibn Ashkab narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya informed me, from al-A'mash, from Muslim ibn Subayh, from Masruq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks with the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound in the heaven like the dragging of a chain on a smooth rock, so they swoon and continue in that state until Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them. When Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to them, ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾, and they say: 'O Jibril, what has your Lord said?' He says: 'He says: the Truth.' Then they call out: 'The Truth, the Truth.'"[[Fath al-Bari 13/382.]][33]

What supports this hadith and explains it is what:

Abu Muhammad 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Faqih informed us, saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishaq ibn Ayyub informed me, saying: Bishr ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: al-Humaydi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: I heard 'Ikrima say: I heard Abu Hurayra say: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain on smooth rock. When ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'To the one who said: ﴿the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great﴾.'"[[Sahih al-Bukhari: 6/28.]][34]

'Aqil ibn Muhammad informed me, from al-Mu'afa ibn Zakariyya, from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, from Zakariyya ibn Aban al-Misri, from Nu'aym, from al-Walid ibn Muslim, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, from Abu Zakariyya, from Raja' ibn Haywa, from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "When the people of the heavens hear that, they swoon and fall down prostrate to Allah. The first to raise his head will be Jibril, and Allah will speak to him with His revelation what He wills. Then Jibril passes by the angels; every time he passes a heaven, its angels ask him: 'What has our Lord said, O Jibril?' Jibril says: 'He said the Truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.' He said: They all say the same as what Jibril said. Then Jibril arrives with the revelation at the place where Allah commanded."[[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/94.]][35]

And with this chain, from Ibn Jarir, from Ya'qub, from Ibn 'Ulayya, from Ayyub, from Hisham, from 'Urwa, who said: al-Harith ibn Hisham said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How does the revelation come to you?" He said: "It comes to me like the sound of a bell, and it departs from me when it departs, and I have memorized what it said. And sometimes it comes to me in the form of a man, and he speaks to me, and that is easier for me."[[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 22/111.]][36]

Some of them said: they are startled out of fear of the Hour arriving.

Al-Kalbi said: "Between 'Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them both) there was a long interval, lasting five hundred and fifty years, in which no messengers came. When Allah sent Muhammad (peace be upon him), Allah spoke to Jibril about the message to Muhammad. When the angels heard the sound, they thought the Hour had arrived, and they swooned at what they heard. When Jibril descended, he began to pass by the people of each heaven, and the fear was lifted from them, so they raised their heads, and one of them said to another:"

What did your Lord say? They did not know what He had said, but they replied: "He has said the truth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great." That is because Muhammad, in the eyes of the people of the heavens, was among the signs of the Hour. When God the Exalted sent him, the people of the heavens were terrified, and they had no doubt that it was the Hour.

Al-Dahhak said: The angels "who succeed one another" (al-mu'aqqibat), who go back and forth among the people of the earth and record their deeds, when the Lord sends them down, descend with a loud sound. Those who are below the angels suppose that it is something from the affair of the Hour, so they fall down prostrate and swoon, until they realise that it is not from the affair of the Hour. This is a warning from God, the Glorified, and an informing that the angels, in this state, cannot intercede for anyone except with His permission. When God gives them permission and they hear His revelation, this is their condition. How then could idols intercede?

Others said: Rather, those described by this are the polytheists.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said, meaning: "Until, when the terror is removed from the hearts of the polytheists at the coming of death upon them, as a establishment of proof against them, the angels will say to them: 'What did your Lord say in the world?' They will say: 'The truth.' They acknowledge it when acknowledgment no longer benefits them. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying, at the end of the surah: ﴿And if you could see when they are terrified, and there is no escape﴾ [Saba': 51].
